#6751. Bella Hadid’s Radical Vulnerability

Every product on this page was chosen by a Harper's BAZAAR editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

How do you stay open in an industry that demands toughness? Bella Hadid embarks on a new chapter with a renewed sense of optimism and her boundaries firmly in place.

I first met Bella Hadid on a fashion shoot I was styling more than a decade ago. We went on to shoot several stories together, including her first major American magazine cover. On one of those shoots, she arrived upset because she had just found out she didn’t get cast in the Victoria’s Secret show. I will never forget telling Bella that one day, Victoria’s Secret would be begging her to walk for them. Cut to today, and Bella is not only one of the most in-demand models, but she opened their most recent show. When I saw her hit the runway in a beaded floral bra and matching wings, I let out a scream because I knew what that moment meant to her.

A few days after the Victoria’s Secret show in October, Bella and I sat down to reflect on her career so far, forgiveness and success, turning 30, and where she goes from here. I have always felt connected to Bella because she, like me, is a heart-on-her-sleeve kind of gal. She is deeply vulnerable and human, and it’s what makes her one of the most compelling figures in fashion today.

Samira Nasr: This is a full-circle moment. On one of our first shoots together, you were really upset because you didn’t get the Victoria’s Secret show. And I said to you, “One day, they will be begging you to be in their show.” And I could tell you didn’t believe me. Your whole body shut down. And three days ago, you opened Victoria’s Secret. Holy shit.

Bella Hadid: I still don’t believe you, to be honest. I feel like people are just AI-ing me onto the runway. I think that it’s so crazy how time passes and you still have some kind of impostor syndrome. No matter how hard you work, there’s always another girl who is more deserving, more beautiful, and has worked so hard to be able to get that spot. Ten years ago, I remember that moment too, where I never thought I would get the show, but I think that God always has a plan, and I truly believe at that time I wasn’t ready. I don’t think I’ve been ready until this year, to be honest. In past years, I was going to my horse-show finals in the morning, flying straight to the Victoria’s Secret show that day, doing rehearsal right before, and then pulling what we call a Bella, and Belinda comes out, and we just act. But this year, I felt really strong.

I have had to make a decision for myself to have boundaries with my own health. And I think it’s gotten me to this point now where I’m able to do the jobs that I do want to do with people that I love, that I can feel inspired by. And that’s truly what [working in] fashion is about: being around people you feel inspired by. Until you find that inspiration, it’s hard to go back into our industry. I think I needed a little bit of time just to be able to be like, “Let me just remember why I’m doing this again,” because I know I’m more than just a face.

SN: We don’t really support a culture of care. I have always believed that boundaries are bridges.

BH: They really are. We know so many people who have been working for 30, 40, 50 years in this industry with zero boundaries. I’ve watched people over the years just get more depressed because they don’t know themselves and they don’t know who they are. And that’s how I was for 10 years, when I didn’t know what my favorite color was, what I liked to eat. I stopped listening to music. To not be able to know yourself in an industry that tells you how to be every single day is really hard.

SN: Going back to Victoria’s Secret, did you feel empowered, or was that your alter ego? What is her name again?

BH: Belinda. You know what? Fortunately and unfortunately, I think it was Bella this year.

BH: I made up my alter ego, Belinda, a long time ago to deal with the intensity of everything happening in my life. So she could deal with that, and I can deal with this, and we can do this together, which I’m realizing I should probably go to therapy about again. Belinda is the one that people are like, “Wow, this, that.”

I have POTS [postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome], and I have a lot of PMDD [premenstrual dysphoric disorder], endometriosis, plus my Lyme and things that affect my body very deeply. Right before I walked out on the runway for my opening look, I went to go stretch and my whole clavicle completely … I don’t even know what it was. My lungs almost collapsed, and I couldn’t breathe, and then it was like, “Five, four …” So my body goes through these different motions of feeling really good and then all of a sudden crashing on me at the worst moments. I need to realize maybe my body can’t handle all that I have going on. Because I know how to walk. One thing I can do is I can strut. But it’s a lot of pressure; we all have our own insecurities. Sometimes my body just can’t connect with my brain. My brain wants to do it, and my body is like, “No, we can’t do that today.” And I’m like, “Okay, great. So let’s figure out another way.” But I think people don’t realize how much I struggle with the fatigue and the body pain, and so I just try my best.

SN: You’ve achieved so much in your 20s. You just turned 30. What are you looking forward to in your 30s?

BH: It’s funny, today I woke up with—I wouldn’t say the word is anxiety, but this feeling of “Oh my gosh, my life is starting.” I want to get rid of what doesn’t bring me joy and bring in what does. I’ve tried to put myself in positions for work for a very long time that have made me feel out of body or like I don’t belong. Years ago, I was just grateful to get a job, and I would say yes to everything. I lacked boundaries then, but I do believe that that gave me the strength to be able to have the confidence in my own boundaries now. I’ve achieved pretty much all the goals that I wanted to when it comes to fashion as a model. And now I do want to go into other ventures to eventually get to peace and happiness and love within this universe that God has put me in.

In the next couple of years, it’s just about getting back to community, getting back to using my voice again. I got beaten down pretty heavy for a long time, which pushed me into this very big struggle with my physical and emotional health, which makes my brain turn off and makes me not be able to write or read. When you’re not around enough people that are like-minded, you feel really ostracized. That’s almost where I got to. Of course, I always want to speak from my heart, which I hope will never disrespect anybody, but still be able to have the confidence to speak my truth and hope that people will walk beside me along the way when it comes to that.

SN: Is there something you’re most proud of achieving?

BH: Well, first and foremost, starting [my fragrance line] Orebella was something that I truly needed for my own creativity and to be able to build community. I am not a 50/50 person. I’m an all-in type of girl. Being able to move forward into my 30s, really focusing on building the things that I’ve started—Orebella was something that I pushed so hard for since 2018, and the fact that it’s really now coming to fruition makes me so proud.

When I was 17, going to my first go-see with a stylist I will not name, I was basically told I was too big to wear Saint Laurent and needed to lose a couple of pounds. And that’s when I was just a baby coming out of high school. Twelve years later, now I’m the face of Saint Laurent. I’m the face of Prada, which is incredible and insane. Times have changed so much, and the people that have come into the industry to make it a better place for us as models are so important. Not that that comment ever impacted me. I went through enough struggles with my body before that, so by the time she said that, I was like, “Okay, girl, I’m actually coming out of something that I dealt with very heavily when it came to my body. And now I look at food in a different way, and I love my body, and that’s okay if you think that I don’t look the way that you think I should look.”

I just would love for everyone to think about if every day they had to walk outside and be photographed, what that would feel like, because it’s an uncomfortable feeling for anybody. My face would change so much. I would be super puffy one day, and one day I would look yellow and emaciated, and people would think I was on drugs or doing this or that. And when anybody knows about, one, hormones, just as a woman in general, and two, about immune problems and how weight fluctuates—again, I just think that there needs to be more sensitivity in our industry.

SN: I’m curious if you’ve always been this person—so sensitive, empathetic—from a little girl.

BH: I’ve always felt like my sensitivity and my openness were a disservice to myself because I felt like no one else was like me in those ways, so I shut it down. Now I realize that there is a generosity of thoughtfulness that is so much deeper than just buying somebody an expensive gift. I think sitting on the side of the street with somebody, even if you don’t have any money, is more important than just walking by without caring.

SN: You’re able to access compassion when a lot of people can’t, and that is a superpower. I want to talk about style because you mentioned your archive. I remember you once mentioned you collect Gaultier. Do you still collect?

BH: I do collect. Behind me are bags to sell. But downstairs, I have my Gaultier dress that the atelier made. It was a Naomi Campbell dress that she had worn in one of their shows, and I was obsessed with it. I called their PR, and within a week and a half, because that dress was in a museum, I had it made and sent to Cannes, and that was that white-and-black dress that I wore on the carpet. And so, that’s here. My Coperni dress is here. I have a whole section for Virgil [Abloh].

SN: The last time I saw Virgil was with you, actually.

BH: I don’t think I’ve done a real, full Fashion Month since he passed away. And Vivienne [Westwood] and Karl [Lagerfeld] passed, and I felt like all of my idols were leaving, and it felt really scary. I have all the art Virgil gave me, his letter he wrote me, his bags, his shoes he made me. And then I have my Prada area, my Cavalli area, my Bob Mackies that I’ve been collecting over the years.

BH: Hopefully for a future wedding. There are just some dresses you can’t find again. And Bob did it best.

SN: He’s an American icon. I wanted to talk to you about Cannes. You’re such a queen of Cannes now, and I look forward to seeing you there. Is it fun?

BH: This past year was fun. I felt grounded. To do the red carpet and feel, in those moments, sober and happy and healthy and strong, and go to sleep not having anxiety about going out or how I’m going to look the next day, and just being with loved ones. It did really well for me this year.

Cannes has always held a very special place in my heart. It begins long before I arrive. Working closely with designers on custom gowns, exchanging references, and watching those first sketches come to life is such a beautiful part of the experience.

This year, being there to support Marie-Clémentine Dusabejambo’s Ben’Imana, the first Rwandan film in the official selection, was especially meaningful. It explores memory and reconciliation after the genocide against the Tutsi through women whose lives carry its legacy. That’s what I love about cinema: It brings us closer and gives stories too rarely heard the attention they deserve. You can enter a theater knowing nothing of someone’s world and leave carrying a little of it with you.

SN: I look at you and how hard you’ve worked for so long, from our first job together. To me, it feels like you’ve achieved so much. But what does success look like for you? Do you feel you’ve achieved it?

BH: I talked to my business manager yesterday, so that made me feel a little bit more successful. But when you don’t think about the money part of it, I think success truly comes from peace within. At the end of the day, I really don’t need much. That’s why I do give back so much, because a lot of the money that I do make, I don’t feel deserving of. There are so many people in the world, whether it’s doctors or teachers, that I think deserve my pay rate a lot more than I do.

From an external space, success is about how known you are, how much you make, how many times you can be on TV, how many covers you’re on, how many fashion shows you do. And that is really important in our industry, especially when you’re building. But for me, I am different. Success, for me, can be living in peace, in a small town, with a man that I love, with my child, having my animals. I’ve always wanted to start a farm-to-table bakery, with flowers, and everything comes from the community. I want to do things that are fulfilling for me in my soul: having a greenhouse that I can garden in, having my glassblowing and ceramic studio, and having lots of children and being a mother. It wasn’t a dream that I’ve always had, but it’s something that now is so intense for me. My intuition is screaming so loudly at me about it.

I think knowing there is a reason behind everything is so important. My sister and I donated a million dollars to Palestine last year [the donation was split between HEAL Palestine, Palestine Children’s Relief Fund, World Central Kitchen, and United Nations Relief and Works Agency], which we could have never been able to do without the success that we’ve had.

God gave me the platform to be able to speak about the things that I hold dearly to me. And when it comes to Palestine or Sudan or Congo or Rwanda or places that mean so much to not only myself but the people around me—to give people a voice in any capacity, that’s success for me as well. To make my family wide and far proud, or to see themselves in me, it gives me strength.

This story appears in the Winter issue of Harper’s Bazaar.

#6750. The Best Gold Nail Polishes, From Soft Champagne to Molten Chrome

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

Gold nail polish has a way of making any manicure feel intentional. It can read as quiet luxury on a bare hand, as festive sparkle at a holiday party, or as a modern accent against deep neutrals. But “gold” isn’t one shade. It’s a whole family, and the right pick depends on your skin tone, your style, and the finish you love.

Some golds are warm and buttery, with a champagne glow that flatters nearly everyone. Others lean rich and antique, with the weight of real metal. Then there are glitter-packed formulas that catch the light with every movement, and chrome finishes that look like liquid foil poured over your nails.

To save you the trial and error, we’ve rounded up the best gold nail polish colors, from soft, sheer shimmers to bold metallics that make a statement. Whether you want a subtle hint of shine for everyday wear or a standout shade for the season’s celebrations, there’s a gold here worth adding to your collection.

#6743. Louis Vuitton Takes Its Place at the Formula 1 Las Vegas Grand Prix Finish Line

A handcrafted trunk awaited the winner, Max Verstappen.

When Max Verstappen crossed the finish line at the Las Vegas Formula 1 Grand Prix on Saturday night, after a gripping race that saw the championship driver battle to maintain the tightest of leads against rivals George Russell and Kimi Antonelli, his trophy came in very special packaging: a bespoke Louis Vuitton trunk. For the past two seasons, Trophy Trunks have been presented to the winner of the annual Las Vegas event, which sees drivers race on a thrilling course that winds along the famous Strip. They have also been presented to the winners of the World Cup, America’s Cup, and the NBA Finals. Louis Vuitton had a strong presence across the whole race weekend, hosting a suite where guests including Teyana Taylor watched the events from above the track and were able to get an early look at the trunk.

The Las Vegas trunk was, like all Louis Vuitton custom pieces, made at Asnières-sur-Seine, a commune in northern France. It was handcrafted by 25 artisans, made to the specific dimensions of the trophy. The Trophy Trunks are a remarkable mingling of the old and the new. They use the traditional craftsmanship techniques that have defined the house for over 170 years. All construction of the trunks’ wood, leather, and locks was done with the same techniques LV has used since the beginning, meaning that in many ways the Trophy Trunks differ little from its trunks from a century ago. The modern energy of motor racing comes through via subtle touches like the two stripes across the trunk that make a large V, a nod to both Vuitton and victory—they’re black-and-white checkered as a nod to the Formula 1 finish line. A small badge that calls back to the early days of trunk travel and bears the winning driver’s initials was added this year.

Louis Vuitton’s relationship with Formula 1 began with the Grand Prix de Monaco, which the brand began creating Trophy Trunks for in 2021. In 2025, it became an official partner of the league, and this year, LV created trunks for all 24 of the season’s races. In early December, the Abu Dhabi Grand Prix will mark the final 2026 race.

#6742. Is This Department Stores’ Big Comeback Christmas?

Gone are the days of the branded luxury Christmas window.

In an era where department stores need to work harder than ever to get a holiday shopper into their store — rather than them shopping online, directly with a brand, or at the department store up the road — many retailers are branching out beyond the monobrand Christmas window strategy that’s dominated recent holiday seasons.

Last week, stores from Bergdorf Goodman to Bloomingdale’s made a splash with their holiday window unveilings. Saks followed suit on Monday, November 23. The weather was unseasonably warm, with attendees clad in light jackets, rather than the usual fur and puffers for this time of year. Bergdorf made up for the tepid temps with fake snow. Bloomingdale’s had Sienna Spiro sing a rendition of “Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas”.

By going the multibrand route, stores can put themselves at the center of their holiday storytelling, and appeal to a wider range of consumers by displaying merchandise across a host of different price points. Utilizing existing merchandise is also a lower lift than the logistical and financial burden of staging a full brand takeover. “I’m anticipating highly creative windows with a variety of merchandise. The general sentiment as of the last several months is that the customer shops high and low, where two years ago it was all about the big labels,” says luxury consultant Robert Burke. “So I think you’re going to see a variety of merchandise displayed in creative ways.”

It’s panning out. Nordstrom is partnering with David Bowie’s estate to celebrate what would be the star’s 80th birthday — and is Nordstrom’s 125th anniversary. Included in Bowie80 are collaborations with designers including Paul Smith, Marc Jacobs and Undercover’s Jun Takahashi. Bergdorf Goodman’s windows are a vignette inspired by a New York winter, celebrating 125 years with an array of capsules from brands including Michael Kors, Brunello Cucinelli and Valentino. Saks’s windows offer up a tour of the festive period in the city. Over in London, Liberty is leaning into storytelling around holiday rituals and routines, and Selfridges is, like its peers, celebrating wintertime in the city (New York City, that is).

Bergdorf invited a host of designers to participate in its holiday window unveiling.

Not all of the players are going wide, though. Bloomingdale’s Friday window unveiling was in partnership with Ralph Lauren. Partnering with Ralph was a no-brainer, says Kevin Harter, VP of integrated marketing. “Ralph Lauren is synonymous with the traditions, nostalgia and timelessness that makes the holidays so special,” she says. The evening included a festive Ralph cocktail in the store — with teddy bear sweaters aplenty — and David Lauren was onstage to celebrate the unveiling alongside Bloomingdale’s CEO Olivier Bron. Inside, though, there are an array of brand activations — over 50 — from Barbour’s Tea & Sympathy pop-up to Ugg’s takeover of the Bloomingdale’s restaurant — and famed froyo destination — Forty Carrots. (There’s an Ugg-exclusive flavor, of course.) Ralph Lauren is the anchor, Harter says.

Overall, this multibrand, amped-up storytelling logic extends to the in-store experience itself. Department stores this season have built out their holiday strategies around curation, with the view of inspiring their customers with the creative while making their lives as easy as possible. “One of the biggest opportunities for retail at Christmas is getting the balance between inspiration and ease right,” says Lydia King, managing director of retail at Liberty.

This is especially important this year, after department stores weathered quieter holiday seasons amid the upheaval of recent years. 2026 started with a bang, as Saks Global declared bankruptcy in January and, since summer, has been pushing its comeback as Exemplar Luxury Group. Bloomingdale’s, too, has spent 2026 pushing upmarket, making the most of a moment in which many of its contemporaries are struggling to meet the moment. This festive period, the stakes are high, capping off a year in which US department stores sought to regain lost magic.

Here’s how department stores are meeting the moment for this all-important holiday season.

This season, retailers are placing emphasis on their curation for the holiday period. The single-brand focus made sense a few years back when luxury was at its peak, Burke says. But now, he argues, department stores are looking to be more democratic in price point and product. “Compared to a few years ago, I’m seeing a lot of interest in smaller brands and independent brands,” he says. “The luxury customer today, even at the highest level, their mindset is very open to not having to only have major luxury branded merchandise.”

Department stores are curating more than just product, though. Across the board — and in keeping with Gen Z’s desire for shopping experiences that offer meaning and excitement inaccessible via social media — they’re placing emphasis on the unique experiences offered in-store throughout the holidays.

Nordstrom’s holiday facade is an embrace of Bowie.

In doing so, they’re putting themselves at the center of the narrative. Bergdorf Goodman is doing this literally, placing the store in the middle of its New York-themed holiday campaign and window display which, this year, literally leads shoppers inside. “After the sidewalk introduces you to the narrative, it continues through the main doors into a Zhivago-esque wintry snow-laden forest hung with rock crystal chandeliers and a flock of white geese overhead,” says Linda Fargo, SVP of Bergdorf’s fashion office and store presentation.

“This year we’ve put much more emphasis on the whole experience of Christmas at Liberty, beyond the product offering,” says Liberty’s King. The store’s campaign, The Liberty Christmas Chronicles, follows the rituals of the season — preparing, dressing, traveling, gathering, unwinding and eventually resting — with gifting running throughout, of course. “We know customers increasingly value curation, personalization and expertise,” she says.

This comes in via mini in-store experiences, from wreath-making with Diptyque (Liberty’s hero partner in its Atrium section) to build-your-own hampers in the Liberty Food Hall. Other activations include personalized bows with Moët & Chandon, lipstick engraving with Lisa Eldridge and makeup bag embroidery with Westman Atelier.

Selfridges is taking a similar multibrand approach with tailored, ‘only available here’ experiences. With Canada Goose on Duke Street, for instance, the retailer has constructed an Arctic-inspired research outpost with hot chocolates and personalized luggage tags, and the ultra-buzzy Vice City GTA VI pop-up kicked off the retailer’s holiday activities.

“These partnerships help create a Christmas that feels distinctive to Selfridges,” says marketing and experiences director Rebecca Warburton. “We know that people are looking for experiences, opportunities to connect with others and to create memorable moments,” she says, noting that Selfridges looked to offer more reasons for customers to spend time at the store this season.

Saks is leaning into these in-person experiences more than ever. For the first time, L’Avenue at Saks will host breakfast with Santa throughout the season and will transform into Le Chalet, with festive menu programming, on holiday season weekends.

Sienna Spiro performed at the Bloomingdale’s x Ralph Lauren window unveiling.

This curation extends to stores’ gifting options. Beyond offering a smart selection of brands, stores are also thinking more deeply about their non-fashion gifting options, so that customers will shop with them not just for shoes, but for stocking stuffers, too.

Bergdorf Goodman does this well, Burke says, noting the store’s “tremendous” holiday season in 2025. “Bergdorf’s home floor is a very good example of it being a tourist destination with fun Christmas merchandise, because they sell all of these Christmas ornaments, candies and candles. It takes over the entire seventh floor,” he says. In celebration of its 125th anniversary, Bergdorf is upping the ante this year with an Assouline legacy book, Very Bergdorf, ‘Very Bergdorf’ specialty ornaments, plus a snow globe featuring the Bergdorf Goodman facade. “Every part of the store has something uniquely made for us, and it all adds up to a very Bergdorf holiday,” Fargo says.

This year, Nordstrom is partnering with toy companies including FAO Schwarz and Jellycats. “You think about a retailer being relevant and having all the things customers want to buy — particularly at the holidays — partnerships like that help, in addition to carrying the best brands in the world,” says Deniz Anders, EVP, chief marketing officer. “Being able to check off their list for everyone across the family, that’s something that we’re really focused on.” Nordstrom has also invested more in consumables this year, and has a partnership with fashion-favorite Flamingo Estate.

This season, department stores are thinking more than ever about ease. Saving customers time and effort, execs believe, is the way to capture their hearts — and their spend.

Nordstrom has expanded its gift shops in common areas throughout the store. “It’s really not something that we used to do, but we want customers to know this is a place that you can buy gifts at broad price points,” Anders says. The retailer tested the cross-store setup last year and has expanded the size of the shops this season. “We want to make it easy and fun for customers to buy gifts.”

Liberty’s largest holiday season development is the introduction of its Gifting Curator service, King says. “For the first time, customers can book one-to-one appointments with Liberty experts who can guide them across the whole store, rather than within a single category or brand,” she says. “The idea is to make discovering the right present feel as special as giving it.” To round out the experience, Liberty has introduced a gift-wrapping experience with wrapper Roxy Wraps.

Stores have also been planting seeds to get their customers in the shopping mindset. Though all of the big, splashy window displays were unveiled at their usual time, just before Thanksgiving, the communications around the holiday season started far earlier. Nordstrom sent out its holiday catalog a week earlier than usual, Anders says. It’s the retailer’s biggest catalog ever. “We’ve been bringing in gifts a lot earlier,” she says. “Holiday is a marathon and you’ve got to have the gifts early and be ready to serve customers and bring a little joy and fun.”

#6739. All About Gabbriette Bechtel, Matty Healy’s Wife

Matty Healy, lead singer of The 1975, has been in a relationship with model and influencer Gabbriette Bechtel since late 2023. In an interview with Highsnobiety published in March 2024, Bechtel candidly shared her feelings regarding the internet’s constant speculation about them.

“I don’t give a shit. I think it’s hilarious. Go for it. Have fun. People have a lot to say,” she laughed. “You don’t know me at all.”

Arguably, Healy’s most well-known relationship came just before he began seeing Bechtel. From May to June 2023, the singer briefly and memorably dated Taylor Swift. The musicians first met in 2014, and while relationship rumors swirled over the years, the two were never official. Swift’s album, The Tortured Poets Department, has even been rumored to be about Healy.

But he and Bechtel have gotten far more serious over their three years of dating and now—marriage! So, who is Healy’s wife? Ahead, everything to know about Bechtel and her relationship with Healy.

Healy and Bechtel’s relationship timeline begins in September 2023. In some photos obtained by People, the pair is seen kissing, hugging, and holding hands while walking together in New York City.

They continued to have PDA sightings, like in November, when they were spotted with their arms wrapped around each other in New York.

Things seem to be getting serious between them by February 2024, when Bechtel was seen spending time with Healy’s family. Photos came out of Healy and Bechtel heading to the theater to watch his mother Denise Welch’s play The Gap. Also in attendance was Healy’s brother, as well as his father, Tim Healy, and his wife.

Previously, in October 2023, Welch showed Bechtel some support on her Instagram. When the model posted a photo wearing nothing but a G-string thong and leather apron from her collaboration with R & M Leathers, Healy’s mom commented, “That’s exactly how I hope to look in mine when it arrives!! 👍👍👍❤️❤️❤️.”

On June 11, the couple announced they were engaged after attending Charli XCX’s Brat Tour show in Brooklyn. Bechtel shared photos of herself wearing the ring, which she was first spotted wearing in May, according to People. The ring has a black diamond in the center that is surrounded by white diamonds.

“MARRYING THE 1975 IS VERY BRAT,” she wrote in the caption.

Denise Welch, Healy’s mom, confirmed the engagement on Loose Women the following day.

“I obviously have known for a few weeks that Matty got engaged,” she said. “They went over to see their friends Charli and George in New York [last night] and I woke up this morning to the fact they’ve put it on Instagram. Instagram official...he’s got engaged to Gabriella Bechtel—Gabbriette she’s known as. Black diamond; he had it made for her...I couldn’t be more thrilled. We couldn’t be happier—she is everything I would want in a daughter-in-law. I’m thrilled.”

The couple was photographed at the O2 Silver Clef Awards on Friday, July 5, sharing a quiet conversation outside Grosvenor House Hotel in London. Bechtel leaned into Healy and kissed him on his cheek. The 1975 frontman was wearing a navy blazer with jeans, and the model wore a black dress with a turtleneck and a pair of black heels. During the ceremony, The 1975 won the Best Group award.

Signaling that they were still going strong in the new year, Bechtel and Healy were spotted on a date in Los Angeles on Jan. 9, 2026. They were photographed walking arm-in-arm to Wilde’s for dinner, a restaurant in Los Feliz. They were both dressed casually in jeans, with Healy wearing a dark cardigan over a white T-shirt and Bechtel in a blazer with rows of gold buttons.

On July 18, Healy and Bechtel were married in Los Angeles at Castillo del Lago, which was formerly owned by Madonna. They appeared kissing at the altar in photos. Bechtel wore a long-sleeve gown with a drop waist and a full floor-length skirt. She had her hair half up with a veil pinned in back. Healy wore a classic black tux and bow tie.

“Matty Healy and Gabbriette Bechtel were married yesterday at a private ceremony in Los Angeles, attended by their family and close friends,” reps for the couple told People.

In an August 2026 interview with Harper’s Bazaar, Bechtel opened up about her impressions of married life with Healy.

“I don’t feel like it’s gonna be very different,” she said. “I feel like I’ve already met my best friend.…The wedding is for our moms and dads. I wanted to do, like, a 50-person thing in a field, so.”

In November 2026, Bechtel and Healy were photographed together in Los Angeles while attending Jessie Jo Stark’s Muse album release celebration. The couple’s outing sparked pregnancy rumors on social media.

Days later, on November 22, People reported that Bechtel and Healy were expecting their first baby together. The news came after the couple was snapped shopping at Bristol Farms in West Hollywood, with Bechtel’s pregnant figure visible in a fitted black dress.

In a May 2023 interview with Vogue, Bechtel shared that she was born and raised in Orange County, and originally moved to Los Angeles to pursue her dream of becoming a professional ballerina.

“I was convinced I was going to be a professional ballerina, and I still am,” she said.

However, her career plans shifted after she was cast by MTV to dance in music videos for Blood Orange (Dev Hynes).

“I put a few dance videos on my Instagram, and somebody reached out to me and said that Dev was having an open call,” she told Highsnobiety. “We had a few fun days of rehearsal and started to film the music video, and then I got a call that I was cut. I didn’t make it into the music video, but I did all of the rehearsals, and I think my feet are in it at some point.”

“I was an unpaid, hard-working model for a very long time,” Bechtel revealed.

Now, Bechtel has modeled for brands like Heaven by Marc Jacobs, Diesel, Miu Miu, and Betsey Johnson. On April 15, 2024, she graced the cover of HommeGirls.

Bechtel is multitalented. In 2019, she was handpicked by Charli XCX to be the lead singer of a band called Nasty Cherry for a Netflix documentary series, I’m with the Band: Nasty Cherry.

“I met [Charli XCX] on the set of a music video, and we ended up partying together for a few years,” she recalls. “I didn’t see her for a while, and then she reached out and was like, ‘I’m doing this project and I’ve been trying to cast the singer…’” Bechtel told Highsnobiety.

Unfortunately, Nasty Cherry is no longer active, with the group choosing to disband during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“We couldn’t do anything together, we couldn’t tour our second EP, and we weren’t able to make music together because we were all in different places in the world. So we just decided that it wasn’t going to work out anymore,” she revealed. “I miss it all the time. It ended too abruptly.”

Bechtel also has a social media presence. Aside from her 1.6 million followers on Instagram, she has amassed 840,400 on TikTok, where she mostly posts cooking videos. In May 2023, she posted a video recreating Erewhon’s grain-free vegan blackout cake, which garnered 3 million views.

Per Highsnobiety, Bechtel shared that she got her love of cooking from her Mexican mother and Swiss-German father, both of whom would cook food from their respective cultures.

“We ate dinner together as a family every single night, so there was always a fresh meal. We never had takeout,” she recalled. “We had a lot of Bon Appétit magazines lying around, so [my mother] would always try new recipes. I would come home and she’d have it open and be like, ‘I’m making this tonight,’ and she’d nail it. I would help her prep, so I grew up with my mom testing out stuff.”

She also shared with Vogue that she is working on a cookbook and eventually would love to open up her own café.

“Not many people know this, but I’m really into interior design. So I’d love to open a space so people can have the full experience,” Bechtel said.

Bechtel was born on July 28, 1997, making her a Leo. Healy, 37, was born on April 8, making him an Aries. According to the AstroTwins, per ELLE.com, “A pair of dynamic fire signs, Aries and Leo make a head-turning duo that whips up passion, adventure, and a heavy dose of drama everywhere you go. A flashy, outspoken pair, you’ll inspire envy. Get ready to reinvent the rules of relationships since your connection is certain to play by its own bold agenda.”

#6737. Inside Fashion’s $276 Billion Succession Shakeup

What appears to be a succession story at a handful of prominent luxury companies is, in fact, a defining moment for the wider industry, with the potential to reshape fashion’s competitive map, a new report says.

“Succession is one of the 10 themes that we believe will shape fashion in the next decade,” says the report’s author, Achim Berg, who in 2025 created FashionSights, a research and advisory boutique, after 23 years at McKinsey.

The report “Fashion’s Succession Problem: The Generational Transfer Reshaping the Industry” is an excerpt from a book Berg co-wrote with Paula Trus titled The Future of Fashion. It is set for publication in March by Bocconi University Press. Ahead of its release, Berg shares the report’s key findings with Vogue Business.

Vogue: Why is succession a defining theme of the next decade?

Achim Berg: We built our index while writing the book. It’s called FashionSights Global 100 (FSG100), a database of the world’s 100 largest fashion and apparel companies ranked by revenue. Out of 100 companies, 46 are family-owned. And out of the 46 companies with family dominance, two-thirds (or 30 companies) face a succession challenge, according to our analysis. These 30 companies generated a combined $276 billion in revenues in 2025. The main criteria for companies meeting what we call succession risk is that they are led by the first or second generation, and those who are in charge, which could be advisory, supervisory board or management, are 65 or older. We also added companies that have publicly acknowledged a succession challenge. It’s worth noting that 63% of the companies navigating succession challenges are based in Europe, 30% in North America and the remaining 7% in Asia-Pacific.

Why is this great generational transfer now?

Most of those companies that are around now, with a few exceptions, were founded in the ’60s, ’70s, ’80s, or ’90s of the last century. Ralph Lauren sold his first ties in 1967. In 1975, Amancio Ortega opened his first Zara store. And in 1984, Tadashi Yanai opened the first Uniqlo store. Modern fashion retail is 60 years old.

Either the family has more than 50% share capital, or more than 50% of the voting rights. But also, in some cases, they do not even need to have that much because they are still the biggest shareholders and they call the shots. Some families have special voting rights or legal structures that allow them to play a larger role.

What are some of the ways succession will play out for these companies?

It depends. First, will the departing owner hand over on time? And second, are the heirs as capable as the founders? Succession will occupy a lot of time and energy, and that could derail some of those businesses. Some of that trouble will lead them to M&A in whatever shape and form. Generational handover could accelerate consolidation as families consider partnerships, outside investment or a sale.  We’re only looking at 30 of the largest 100 companies. But you will also find many smaller businesses facing similar succession challenges and looking to sell. It’s not a given that they’re all going to find an acquirer.

When it comes to buyers, established fashion groups could gain scale through acquisitions and expand their portfolios with new brands. We notably see opportunities for stronger Italian luxury groups.

We also see opportunities for new owners from the beauty and eyewear industries. Think about L’Oréal and EssilorLuxottica and the discussion around Armani. They were considered suitable acquirers by Mr Armani himself.  It could also be a good opportunity for those companies to become more relevant in the fashion space.

Last but not least, brand ownership and licensing companies such as ABG, WHP Global and Marquee Brands could offer another route for families seeking an exit. I interviewed [ABG founder and executive chairman] Jamie Salter for my book. He claims publicly that his ecosystem generates $38 billion in annual retail sales by now. So they can do massive acquisitions globally, and they’re looking for global brands to create licensing.

Some successions, however, are expected to proceed smoothly, according to the report.

Yes, the report identifies clear responsibilities, independent oversight and successors tested through meaningful experience as a foundation for successful handovers.  In the white paper, you will see that we consider the handover at Zegna as one of those more positive examples.  Gildo Zegna is the group executive chair. Gianluca Tagliabue is the group CEO. And Gildo Zegna’s two sons, Edoardo and Angelo Zegna, are also now playing a role as co-CEOs of the Zegna brand and are groomed for succession. A succession typically takes 10 to 15 years of preparation, and our observation is that many of the businesses need to seriously engage in those preparations.

#6736. How Am I Supposed to Survive the Apocalypse Without My Phone?

Anyone who’s ever been trapped on a stalled subway or a WiFi-less flight knows how screwed we might feel without access to our phones. Last week’s tech outages––first, a failure of Microsoft’s systems, then, a national grounding of flights, followed by problems from Charles Schwab to Apple iCloud––were a reminder of how fragile our digital infrastructure is, especially at the dawn of AI. Preppers on Reddit, better known for discussing generators and the storage of food, began talking about how to AI–apocalypse proof the devices we’re all so dependent on. “getting serious about my preps with all the cyber attacks going on,” one user wrote. “I work for a security company so I get a front row seat to a lot of the chaos. I’m specifically prepping for prolonged loss of power.”

Many found their way to Nomad, a pocket-sized device created to aid in offline situations. “I had huge, huge spikes in traffic,” said Jackson Studner, creator of Nomad and a student at Millersville University of Pennsylvania. (“I’m not a company or a startup, just a college student who enjoys building useful things and sharing them,” Studner’s website reads.) With the help of his professors, he built Nomad to provide some entertainment on camping trips and cross-country trips with friends. They’d hit a dead zone, and realize they wanted to watch a movie, or run video game software. Nomad is a miniscule server with TV and films, the entire Wikipedia library, and portable Wi-Fi, and offline maps. “I really like the reliability aspect,” Studner tells me. “I like to own my stuff. It's kind of that simple.” He’s also added navigation for his new community preparing for the apocalypse (or at least a grid shutdown). “It will actually tell you how to go along the road, it can tell you how to walk there, it'll calculate times, that kind of stuff,” he said.

Elsewhere, there are emergency libraries that you can download to your existing computer, with offline chatbots that can tell you how to find clean water or start a fire: lastbook.org, which includes how-to videos; Survival LLM, which offers up information from the CDC and FEMA; and Project Nomad (different from Studner’s Nomad), from Chris Sherwood, a prominent YouTuber. Sherwood is best known for posting explainer videos showing viewers how to build their “homelabs”—personal, at-home computing devices—under the name Crosstalk Solutions.

The interest in Project Nomad, Sherwood said, has been overwhelming. “It’s got over 40,000 stars on GitHub, which means that 40,000 people not only saw the project and were on the page, but they clicked the little button to favorite it. And I'm getting over 200,000 views on the website per month,” he said.

Despite his new fans, Sherwood himself isn’t a prepper. He was inspired by the Information Technology Disaster Resource Center (ITDRC), a non-profit that goes into disasters and provides internet services when they are completely down. “I had the opportunity to go on deployment with [ITDRC] when Hurricane Ian came through, and I saw firsthand all these people that were offline. It was a disaster. Getting people back online was almost as important as the food and water supplies that were getting set up to help with the recovery,” he explained.

Studner wasn’t a prepper either–– at first. But since Nomad took off and he’s found himself in more “prepper” corners of the internet, his feelings have slightly changed. “It’s for peace of mind. I have my little go bag. I'm not too, too worried about it, but I like to know that if there ever was a real problem, I'd be okay in that situation.”

#6734. Everything We Know About ‘Dancing With the Stars’ Season 36, Including Its Likely Premiere Date and Rumored Celebs

Dancing With the Stars is officially wrapping up a chaotic and unmissable season 35, and honestly I’m not sure what I’m going to do for the next 12 months. Other than...I guess wait for Dancing With the Stars season 36? The show won’t be waltzing back into our lives until late 2027, and if you want specifics, it’s time for some sleuthing because we’ve figured out the premiere date (and some rumored cast members!).

No date has been set, but the show pretty much always premieres on a Tuesday night in mid-September. The last few seasons delivered premiere dates of September 17, September 16, and September 15. Looking ahead, it seems likely that Dancing With the Stars will premiere on Tuesday, September 14.

Probably not until a few weeks before the premiere. The season 25 cast was announced on September 2, 2026, just 13 days before the show premiered on September 15. Of course, casting rumors were circulating in the weeks before that, but we had to wait a while for the full Good Morning America announcement!

Yes! To the point where we have a whole roundup this way. While nothing is known for sure, one simply has to look at who’s sitting in the current Dancing With the Stars audience to know who’s considering a stint on the show.

Last season we saw the likes of Taylor Hanson, Maura Higgins, and Jenna Dewan in the audience, all of whom signed on for season 35. Meanwhile, this season has featured celeb audience cameos from Jennifer Love Hewitt, Love Island’s Kenzie Annis and Aniya Harvey, and even Miranda Cosgrove.

Probaaaably not. Ever since Mark Ballas’s mom Shirley Ballas showed up to guest judge Halloween Night, there have been some rumors that she could become a full-time judge on DWTS / replace Bruno Tonioli, but it seems unlikely.

For starters, Bruno—who’s been with the show since day one—isn’t ready to retire.

“Bruno knows the noise about Shirley, and the chatter about shaking up the panel,” a source told The Sun. “He has been vocal to everyone: ‘I love the show, I have no plans to walk away or even consider retirement.’ It is about as loud as you can be without saying: ‘Don’t fire me!’”

That said, he “knows how the industry can be,” and the insider emphasizes that “Bruno has seen it many times. It is never about anyone doing something wrong, but keeping the wheels turning and the fans hooked.”

Stay tuned for updates about Dancing With the Stars season 36 as we get ’em!

#6733. Everything Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams Have Said About Their Friendship

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

HBO Max and Crave’s Heated Rivalry has quickly become one of the most-discussed series of the year, catapulting its stars Connor Storrie and Hudson Williams into the celebrity stratosphere. The two actors portray hockey players Shane Hollander (Williams) and Ilya Rozanov (Storrie), who have a secret love affair spanning almost a decade. The series is known for its spicy intimate scenes as well as its beautiful depiction of romantic yearning.

Storrie and Williams have been open in interviews about their experience creating the show, along with their offscreen relationship as they navigate sudden fame together.

“Hudson is my best friend, and I literally can’t fathom doing this without him,” Storrie told W magazine in December 2025. “We were both in similar places in life before this. We quit our jobs within a day of each other. We booked this and flew out the same day. Now it’s turning into two people who are being seen internationally for the first time. This has been the highlight of my life, and meeting Hudson makes that 10 times sweeter.”

Here, everything the two actors have shared about their friendship.

Fans of the show tend to “ship” Williams and Storrie, hoping they end up dating in real life. Storrie addressed this head-on in an interview with Vulture, saying things are strictly platonic.

When asked about the intimate scenes they shot in the show, Storrie said, “For me, it doesn’t feel spicy at all—like, that’s me and my best friend. This is the first time in my life I’m having this many eyes on me. They’ve seen me naked, they’ve seen me kiss, they’ve seen me be in love with a man on-screen—it’s only normal for people to try to transfer that over to mine and Hudson’s real life.” He explained that he intends to keep his private life private, adding, “I feel honored to be able to bring someone to life that so many people feel seen, understood, and represented by, and I think that transcends whoever I’m sleeping with in my real life.”

Williams expressed a similar sentiment to Deadline, saying, “I want queer people telling queer stories, but also, there’s the element of Connor and I—we’re best friends, and we love expressing that physically. You see people who infer or assume, and you kind of have to let that go. But then again, I never wanna stop expressing the love I have for Connor physically, and I’m never really going to, and I think multiple things can be true at once.”

In November 2026, Williams’s interview on The Assembly aired. One of the audience members there asked Williams if he ever had romantic feelings for Storrie. “No,” he replied. “Quickly, me and Connor realized we were, like, platonic soulmates, just completely in love with each other. I think that’s what made our friendship so stable and beautiful, is that we realized we could be completely ourselves, be completely guard down. So, I think the thing that made our relationship as rich as it was is, like, me and that man could cuddle for 10 hours, and it just mean cuddling, just mean we just love each other dearly, but don’t wanna beep each other’s bop.”

He then added playfully, “Who doesn’t want Connor Storrie in their shower? You know, someone needs to get my back. I wish Connor was just with me every day. I’m like, ‘Hey, I have a loofah but I can’t reach [my back].’ If I had Connor with me every day, he could just come in there.”

Sophie Nélisse, who plays Heated Rivalry’s Rose Landry, interviewed Williams for Wonderland magazine in January 2026 and asked him how he and Storrie balance promoting the show with forging their own identities. Williams admitted that they purposely go to different events, in part to keep their friendship more private and their brands separate.

“It’s been really nice, because Connor and I are aligned,” Williams began. “We want to be different artists. We don’t want to be the Olsen twins. We want to be Connor and Hudson, with different filmographies and different deals. As much as we love each other, our friendship doesn’t need to be public. Jacob [Tierney] has that quote: ‘Shane and Ilya are for the public. Connor and Hudson are for themselves.’ And that’s how we feel. People want to see us front row together all the time, but we actively avoid that, because it starts to feel like branding. If you’re always seen together, you become attached at the hip. I FaceTime him whenever I’m free. But if we’re offered the same fashion shows, we’re like, ‘Which one are you going to? Okay, I’ll go to a different one.’ We’re stubborn, selfish artists who want to be our own people. We’re like, ‘I love you. I don’t want to do everything with you.’”

Both Williams and Storrie got into great shape for the show. In a profile with GQ in December 2025, Williams talked about meeting his co-star and being intimidated by his build.

“Connor pushed himself up onto the island in the kitchen,” Williams said. “I remember seeing his arms. They were the size of my legs. I was like, Holy fuck.”

“It’s not true,” Storrie responded. “Because you have crazy legs.”

The show’s creator, Jacob Tierney, also commented on their affection for one another in the piece, saying, “They’re living through a thing right now that is bananas—absolutely fucking bananas—and they’re handling it with grace, with humor, with generosity. They adore each other, which is like, thank fucking God.”

While discussing his own workout routine with Men’s Health in January, Williams had a playful quip about Storrie’s physique: “I’m okay talking about my butt, but poor Connor Storrie—who has the fattest butt I’ve ever seen on a man—I’m sure just wants to stop talking about his beautiful cheeks.”

In a December interview with Entertainment Weekly, the friends discussed a viral video from the Heated Rivalry wrap party where they are rolling around on the floor together.

“Very plainly spoken, me and Hudson are freaks,” Storrie explained. “We’re clowns. We just love to riff and have fun and go crazy, and those were two situations where we were caught off guard doing our thing. The wrap party, that was all improvised. I think we were just putting on a show.”

Williams added, “Also, there might be something else, I think, with—we’re both very physical actors, and movement is a huge part of it.”

During his Vulture interview, Storrie spoke about moving into an apartment next to Williams’s while filming in Toronto.

“We would literally just go to set, go home, cook, work out together, and geek out over how excited we were to finally be working on this level,” he said. “If we were any less close, we probably would’ve gotten annoyed with each other really quick.”

The American actor told Vulture that they leaned into their chemistry while promoting Heated Rivalry’s first season. “If Hudson says something jokingly, like, ‘Spit in my mouth,’ I think that gives everyone else the go-ahead to get in on that too,” he said. “People are ruthless talking about our holes and our butts.”

During his discussion with Interview, Storrie added that spending time with Williams has helped ground them both during their press tour. “Hudson’s been in town, so we’ll have some quality time and come back down to ground zero,” he said. “It’s funny, because all the press and stuff is getting easier and easier and easier. You would think you would get burnt out and exhausted. Even though it’s only been three weeks of doing press for this, I’m clicking into an interesting sort of confidence and appreciation for all of this.”

Williams, meanwhile, credited Storrie for helping him keep the press tour fun during an interview with The Hollywood Reporter. “I have one of my best friends for life right beside me through it all, which is already a luxury that a lot of actors don’t get,” he said. “I’m sure I would’ve probably had a smaller appetite for the amount of stuff we’re doing if I didn’t have him through this. I’m an omnivert, leaning more to an extrovert, but I still get—I have ADHD, I’m unmedicated, currently, for the last while, so my social battery can just tap [out] pretty quick. At the end of the day, I’m pretty forgiving with myself if I’m talking with a reporter in a polite, more boring way. Then when I’ve had coffee, and I’ve had a nap, I let myself be chaotic. I let myself off the leash. I try to say, whatever mood I’m in, just be Canadian, don’t be mean. Whatever they get, they get.”

Timid magazine asked Williams how Storrie’s acting has helped him be a better performer. Williams responded, “He’s so incredibly present and so incredibly truthful. As an actor, it’s so much easier to think of what you should be doing or what you think would be an entertaining version of this or the most dramatic version or make sure you’re hitting these lines properly or doing the scene properly or the director wants this and the script says this. But just to actually listen to the person and let what they’re saying affect you—Connor is so good at that. There’s so many moments where I am saying something and the script says he does this, and he does something so unexpectedly emotional or so unexpectedly vulnerable that even if I’m very robotic and going through a scene, he can crack me and change my trajectory in the scene. He’s a huge resource in affecting me and that makes my job way easier because I don’t have to. He makes me be present. He’s so good at that. That’s his superpower.”

Storrie, meanwhile, credited Williams for helping him understand Ilya so quickly in his Interview story. “I feel like I got the character pretty instantly,” he began. “I believed in his circumstances without almost any effort, and I just trusted Hudson so much. It’s so easy to act when you know where you’re coming from and you believe the person opposite you. I mean, I’m so gooey. I’m such a romantic. So any of the really heightened emotional moments—their love or confession or an outbreak or a fight—those are the moments that I really enjoy as an actor.”

Williams listed out all the nicknames he and Storrie have for each other during his Timid magazine interview. “He calls me Huddy, Papi, Bubba, Baby,” he said. “I call him Pookie. I used to call him Pookie a lot. Papi. Oh, Con Con. I call him that both in text form and verbally. But yeah, a lot of nicknames.”

GQ revealed that when the series wrapped, they got matching tattoos that read “SEX SELLS.”

The Canadian star revealed that he stayed at Storrie’s Los Angeles apartment when he came to the U.S. to do some press. “We were like, ‘Oh, my God, if people saw us just getting ready in the morning, giving each other big spooning hugs, just to say we’re proud of each other,’ people would be going crazy,” he told Variety. “If only one fan had access, God forbid. But yeah, we just love each other very dearly.”

The outlet asked him what creating Heated Rivalry taught him. Williams responded, “I think I had my own biases, maybe that would be too strong of a word, but my own discomfort if I expressed myself fully, physically and affectionately, both with women and men. It would feel inappropriate. I realized if you really do love someone—platonically or not—I’m such a tactile, sensory person. There are so many taboos. It’s much harder on men. I had to let that go, and I got to learn how freeing that is. That also went hand-in-hand with being myself, truly as an artist. Connor was also a great person to have at my side. I think we both opened each other up to just be freer, more fully expressive.”

During Williams’s January 2026 appearance on Andy Cohen Live, he revealed that Storrie is an “awful texter,” but they largely keep in touch with frequent video calls. “We’ll Facetime each other or call each other randomly, very consistently,” he told the host. “That has sort of been my stability, especially through this. Just having my best friend who is in the same position I am.”

In a November 2025 interview with The Permanent Rain Press, Williams said he would pitch Storrie as “a beautiful little, sensitive little radical, artist boy. Who should be treated with the utmost care and hugs and friendliness because he can’t handle anything else. And that’s perfect. And that’s the way he should be treated.”

He added, “And anyone who doesn’t treat him that way should die.”

In May 2026, Williams and Storrie made their Met Gala debut. They took a bathroom selfie together, which Williams later posted to his Threads account.

The pair’s appearance at the Met Gala excited fans, with one user taking a solo shot of Williams and posting it alongside lyrics from Rihanna’s breakup song, “Woo.” (Williams has a longtime girlfriend, Katelyn Larson.) The post has since been taken down, but Williams responded and wrote, “Rpfing [real person fan fiction] gotta stop y’all.”

During his November interview on Vogue’s The Run-Through podcast, Storrie revealed that he and Williams were living together while shooting season 2 of Heated Rivalry.

“Right now we’re filming [the next season of Heated Rivalry], so I literally live with him, which is amazing,” he said. “We were at this hotel, which was a brilliant hotel, but I just….I needed a washing machine. I needed a kitchen.”

Storrie also discussed how their red carpet looks sometimes seem coordinated without any advance planning, pointing to their similar outfits at the Vanity Fair Oscar Party.

“We’ve had a few moments where it just matched. But that’s just very telling of Hudson and I in general. We are very cut from the same cloth. We have a soul tie thing. So there’s a lot of synchronicity. But no, we don’t coordinate before at all,” he said.

He also expressed admiration for Williams’s personal style, particularly his approach to streetwear and tailoring.

“Hudson is really cool. You know what I mean? Hudson has this sort of, there’s something kind of like street style or edgy about what he does,” Storrie explained. “And like when he dresses up, when he does like fine suits and tailoring, it’s a little bit different. And I always kind of envy that, like him being able to wear really cool stuff, because it doesn’t really work the same on me. But I like my thing too.”

#6732. Best Men's Studded Belts 2026: From RRL to Our Legacy

Most people might build an outfit around a pair of shoes. Others, around a jacket. But few, surprisingly, do it around a belt.

At GQ, we’ve always said that the overlooked belt is more than the sum of its buckle and holes. Not only will it stop your slacks from going south, but a good leather belt can make just as much of a statement as your shoes, and deliver as much of a stylistic flourish as a tie. Unconvinced? Enter: The studded belt. (Which, coincidentally, we're now increasingly seeing be offered by some of the most imitated brands in the industry, from Lemaire to RRL, Mfpen to Our Legacy.)

The charm of the studded belt is that it’s a vibe chameleon. Its decorative elements can pay tribute to any number of aesthetics, from Americana to punk to European artistry. And while any one will easily provide further flair to an already-singing outfit, the best ones also single-handedly bring even the most minimalist wardrobe to life. (And to be honest, that’s how I feel studded belts are best worn today: Against a white tee and jeans, for an easy win without changing your whole look.)

To help you find the right one for you, I've sorted through the vast waist-wear market to find a selection that won't just make your outfits sing, but set them on course for superstardom. See you out there, Stud.

Let's start gently: Somehow, Anderson’s has made a studded belt that whispers. It’s a small but mighty addition to their lovingly handcrafted Italian leather goods.

“If a stud falls out, make a wish,” is the outlook over at Htc Los Angeles—and they provide plenty of it. A true purveyor of the style, the brand has been specializing in rock-and-roll embellished leather goods since the ’90s. And they aren’t stingy with it either.

Trust Corridor NYC to come in clutch for all of your folksy Americana needs. The worn-in look of their studded belt—made in full-grain leather and tarnished hardware—carries all the tales of someone who’s worn it through the arid badlands.

If the fits over at the Ralph Lauren PoloFest in Tokyo last month have inspired you to join the RL tribe, any one of the many studded belts from RRL (Ralph's ranch-minded line) is a strong place to start.

As you’ll see from our list, Our Legacy—a staple for any serious fashion guy—has secured two call-outs. Here, they cut diamond studs to form a snakeskin-like pattern that, when worn against your best corduroy pants, gives the look some severe shine.

While we’re talking about studded belts as an easy hardware win, they're also the perfect place to score some color points too. Here, the green and orange mixes it up more than traditional turquoise.

Since its founding in 2012, Maximum Henry has been handmaking our favorite leather goods right here in New York City, including their beloved oval buckle belt. But they also know how to do a good, uncomplicated studded belt.

The floral studs on this OL belt aren’t merely decorative, but are punched into the very function of the eyelets. It’s a sweet look, really, and one done so effortlessly.

Dressing for winter, when all you ever want to feel is cozy, can leave you feeling like a schlub. There is, however, an easy fix in the form of the enviably Parisian stylings of Lemaire, who’ve released a brown belt with almond-shaped studs. Wear it with your all-denim outfit or heavy grey wool pants, it’ll make you feel like one of the brand’s cityslicking models in their closely-studied runway shows.

While we’ve so far been paying attention to how studs can add some play, texture still plays a key role to make an outfit sing. A Kind of Guise made their turquoise studded belt with a tan nubuck leather.

Lemaire might be better known for their artsy fabrics and drape-y cuts, but their accessories department is a treasure trove too.

Florals can be a lot generally for most guys, but Mfpen uses theirs sparingly on their lean 2cm wide belt. Made in patent brown leather, it also adds a nice formal sheen to a dark winter ensemble.

We’ve so far seen how studded belts can sway from Americana to minimalist vibes, but we can’t leave out the heavy metal rockers. Heliot Emil shaves off the edges for something more digestible, but still packs enough punch to cut through a monochromatic outfit.

Finally, we've talked a lot about how to add spice to your fit, but what does that mean—really? Eraldo has some answers.

#6731. Meet ‘Dune: Part Three’’s Ida Brooke, the Young Brit Denis Villeneuve Picked to Play Zendaya’s Daughter

Ida Brooke is wearing a piece of Dune around her neck. The necklace is silver and unassuming, but she explains its provenance: at the end of filming Denis Villeneuve’s Dune: Part Three, silver used in the production was collected, melted down, and recast into wrap gifts for the cast. Brooke hasn’t taken hers off since.

“There’s nothing that’s going to be as good as that,” the 18-year-old actor says, turning it between her fingers over coffee in a central London café. It has changed the rest of her jewelry too: once a gold devotee, today she is wearing a stack of silver rings. (She is otherwise dressed in the Gen-Z uniform of a tank top and low-rise cargo trousers, her hair falling in glossy natural curls.) It feels particularly apt for someone whose life is currently divided into very distinct before and afters. Only a few months ago, she was a film student at the Brit School; soon, audiences will know her as Ghanima, the daughter of Zendaya’s Chani and Timothée Chalamet’s Paul Atreides, opposite Nakoa-Wolf Momoa as her twin brother, Leto II, in Villeneuve’s third Dune film.

To get there was a months-long exercise in trying not to unravel. Brooke initially self-taped without knowing she was auditioning for Dune. When her agent revealed the project, she shut the curtains on a sunny day and watched the first two films back to back. “I fell so in love with it,” she says. “I was like, ‘OK, this is going to really hurt if I don’t get this.’” By the final audition, she had already convinced herself that another girl outside the room had the advantage. Brooke went to the bathroom and gave herself a talking to. “You don’t have to get it,” she remembers thinking. “You just have to show them that you have something to say. Just make their choice a little bit harder.”

The following day, Brooke was sitting beside a teacher at school trying to solve an editing problem when a message flashed up from an unknown number: Villeneuve wanted to call her in 20 minutes. Her phone had five percent battery. She tore through the school searching for a charger, eventually hiding in a stairwell to take the call. He first warned her about the intensity of the shoot—the heat, the physical demands—and asked whether she wanted to join the film. A friend found Brooke crying and took a photograph. “She was like, ‘You might want this one day.’”

Cinema has been the organizing obsession of her life since childhood. At six, she would rewatch films endlessly on a portable DVD player; as a teenager growing up in west London, she traveled across the city for Saturday acting classes. She now lives with her father and younger sibling, a household she affectionately describes as “very rowdy.” A lifelong cinephile, though he doesn’t work in film, her father’s fascination with human psychology has informed her own approach to storytelling. (The two share a love of Martin Scorsese.) “He always loved quality stories and has really good taste,” she says, smiling.

Writing interests her as much as performing: she likes structure, psychology and—gleefully—eavesdropping, listening to “the cadence of how people speak,” she says, gesturing cheekily at the conversations trilling around us. She is currently working on a screenplay exploring Vietnam veterans and the pharmaceutical industry, a project born from the inquisitive way she approaches the world. She will also star in and executive produce an indie drama, Grass Roots, due to shoot next summer.

Calm proved instructive in the desert. Zendaya, who had already endured the elements on the earlier films, helped Brooke understand how to quiet her body enough to perform. “I feel so much more confident acting in somewhat normal environments now,” she says. Learning to act, for Brooke, has also meant learning when to pay attention and when to give in. “Denis has such a vivid imagination that you can step right into his vision… You just have to be a kid.”

Ida Brooke as Ghanima and Nakoa-Wolf Momoa as Leto in Dune: Part Three.

Brooke missed her graduation—and the screening of her final Brit School film, The Operator, which won an award—because she was away filming the forthcoming sci-fi live-action Gundam movie alongside Noah Centineo and Sydney Sweeney in Australia. When she told her new castmates how gutted she was, they improvised a graduation of sorts: everyone piled onto a sofa and screened her film together. “I had that sense of community that I missed.”

For the moment, Brooke is resisting any pressure to decide exactly what she is. Actor? Writer? Director? All three? She chose not to go to university and has instead devised her own education, meeting writers to ask how they work, reading about psychology and screenwriting, watching films, researching whatever historical period has most recently caught her imagination. “One of my biggest priorities is self-education,” she says.

Her necklace is a souvenir from one of the biggest film sets ever conceived, but Brooke looks voraciously forward at what she hasn’t encountered yet. She wants to work with Scorsese, but she also talks excitedly about young, unknown filmmakers in London: “The friends that I have now, I see them as my future colleagues.” Her ambition is not in conquering new terrain, it’s to remain porous enough to keep discovering. After all, silver can always be melted down and made into something new.

#6728. A Rare Alexander McQueen Gem Is Coming to Auction

The iconic Alexander McQueen “Plato’s Atlantis” dress is headlining Christie’s December Luxury Week.

Few remnants of fashion history manage to stir up emotions and draw headlines quite like pieces from Alexander McQueen’s revered runways. Rare, technical, and sensorial, these are certainly not your average, everyday pieces of clothing. McQueen runway pieces are often flexed at the world’s top fashion exhibitions at museums around the world. That’s just one of the reasons why the multicolor silk minidress from Alexander McQueen spring/summer 2010 “Plato’s Atlantis” is the star of Christie’s December Luxury Week, where the runway gem will be hitting the auction block with a $150,000 to $300,000 estimate. The sale runs online from November 25 to December 10, 2026.

“Based on what we know about McQueen’s distribution at the time and the types of garments that went into production after a runway show, we estimate there were probably only fewer than two dozen examples of this exact dress produced,” Max Brownawell, head of handbags at Christie’s, tells ELLE. “Then on top of that, the importance of ‘Plato’s Atlantis,’ as McQueen’s final fully realized collection, really can’t be understated. He himself said that his previous collection was his final as a young man. And so this was his most mature, fully fledged collection that he’d ever produced.”

The dress was the fourth look in the runway collection, styled with the iconic Armadillo boots. Designed with a futuristic sculpted drape, covered in prints from the natural world (think: a collage of abstracted imagery pulled from butterfly wings, snakeskin, and insects), the silhouette is a favorite of fashion fans and archivists. Brownawell shares that the piece still has the tag attached and has likely never been worn. The ensemble may very well exceed the estimate: for reference, a “Plato’s Atlantis” look complete with those aforementioned boots sold for $1.5 million including fees at a Fair Warning auction in New York on Sept. 17, 2026, setting an auction record for McQueen.

“He was going for something that was entirely new,” says Brownawell. “This dress is a really prime example of that, the way that the print has been designed to lay perfectly within the architecture of the garment itself is really a spectacular sort of couture level of creation. On top of that, you have this unbelievably architectural draping, which, you know, McQueen has, it’s been said that he really actually draped a lot of these pieces directly onto the forms themselves because it was so complex.”

Aside from the dress itself, Alexander McQueen’s spring/summer 2010 show was ahead of its time in every way. It was the first show to be livestreamed in real time on the internet, and it was the first fashion show to debut a major pop single during a show; Lady Gaga’s “Bad Romance” premiered during the show’s finale. “McQueen’s legacy has been just growing stronger and stronger every year,” adds Brownawell.

The dress is hitting the auction block at a time when Christie’s is launching its inaugural fashion auction. “We really believe that the market is at a point right now where people do appreciate the important designs,” he says. “There’s a lot of clothing out there, but there’s also a lot of very important pieces that define what we wear and where fashion is going and where it’s been.”
