No AI. 100 per cent Aerie Real,” read the caption accompanying the campaign launch post, which features BTS shots of Aerie’s festive campaign shoot cast and crew. The brand, which previously swore off Photoshop in its campaigns, has been known to centre its messaging around human “realness”; this latest effort underscores how divisive AI-made campaigns have become.

While some advocates for AI images argue they get rid of creative constraints, the biggest backlash against brand experiments with AI-generated images so far has surrounded campaigns that seem like they could have been made without AI. Some analysts say that human-made content will soon become the ultimate marker of luxury. Will more brands follow Aerie’s lead this festive season?

The news: Meta is reportedly laying off 600 employees from its AI division.

Why it matters: Facebook and Instagram owner Meta is cutting some 600 staff from its so-called Superintelligence unit, the company’s AI division, according to multiple reports. The news was first reported by Axios, who cited an internal employee memo. “By reducing the size of our team, fewer conversations will be required to make a decision, and each person will be more load-bearing and have more scope and impact,” Meta’s chief AI officer Alexandr Wang wrote in the memo to employees, according to Axios’s report. It’s a turnaround after the company went on an AI hiring spree earlier this year, that included the hiring of Wang himself, and comes amid broader speculation that the tech industry is heading for an “AI bubble” that has seen AI companies receive mega investment before delivering on business fundamentals. Investors’ eyes will be closely watching Meta’s competitors to see if they soon follow suit.

The news: Frasers Group partners with Commercetools to build out agentic AI capabilities.

Why it matters: In September, ChatGPT launched its “agentic commerce protocol” (ACP), an open-source tech standard that allows various AI agents from companies like Perplexity, Google and Microsoft to interact with each other, connect to different commerce systems and complete purchases, in partnership with Shopify and Commercetools. Now, Frasers Group is working with Commercetools to become one of the first European retailers to roll out two agentic commerce products, AI Hub and Agent Gateway.

The company said this partnership will allow shoppers to discover and purchase products from Frasers Group’s retailers like Sports Direct and Flannels directly within AI shopping channels such as ChatGPT and Google AI when their integrated checkout features land in Europe. It’s the first major announcement from a European retailer indicating an intention to launch AI shopping agents — which would search, select and purchase products on behalf of the customer — when the tech is ready.

The news: Pinterest introduces the option for users to remove AI-generated content from their feeds.

Why it matters: Pinterest’s new controls allow users to personalise their feeds and opt out of seeing AI-generated imagery across specific categories, including home decor and beauty, as well as men’s, women’s and children’s fashion. The tech company said it will also make its existing AI-generated labels more noticeable in the coming days. For Pinterest, it’s a move that indicates just how business-critical transparency is around AI, and gives us an idea of the intensity of the backlash the platform has received against such content — a highly controversial subject when it comes to creative forms like image and video.

The news: Revolve launches AI-powered personal styling tool.

Why it matters: The US multi-brand retailer tapped fashion entrepreneur Sandy Sholl’s AI startup Zelig to power its new ‘Build a Look’ onsite feature. Revolve customers can now mix and match items from the site and style them on digital avatar models — all enabled by Zelig’s combination of generative AI and computer vision, as well as input from IRL stylists, the brands claim. Revolve has also launched a “digital closet” feature for shoppers to save desired items as well as those purchased. It’s the latest personalisation play from an online retailer, as they race to enhance their websites with the latest AI capabilities, to retain engagement as more shoppers adopt AI search. While individual brands like Ralph Lauren and Moncler are investing in bespoke features that replicate their in-store experiences online, for multi-brand players, retaining a USP in the age of AI is an even tougher challenge.

The news: OpenAI’s Sora app hits one million downloads, faster than ChatGPT.

Why it matters: OpenAI exec Bill Peebles, who is in charge of the tech firm’s new Sora video-generation app, announced that Sora reached one million app downloads in under five days — a faster take-up than when the company released ChatGPT in November 2022. It gives us an idea of just how high consumer demand is for visual experiments through AI — the app is currently invite-only and available exclusively to users in North America. It also comes amid creator copyright concerns over the AI’s use of their work. If the app grows rapidly before the company has proper controls and protections in place, there could soon be a vast amount of AI-generated content published with likenesses to original works.

The news: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman promises creators more “granular” controls over Sora 2’s content usage.

Why it matters: Just four days after OpenAI launched Sora 2, its new invite-only video generation app, CEO Sam Altman took to his online blog to promise creators of copyrighted characters more “granular” controls, “similar to the opt-in model for likeness but with additional controls”, over the use of their creations by the app. He said the company had been “taking feedback” from rightsholders and app users and would work to “fix the missteps very quickly” as it develops OpenAI’s video generation tools. This prompt response from Altman reflects just how contentious image use for AI tools is right now, while wider regulation to protect creatives’ IP is yet to be seen. For now, legal experts say for brands wanting to experiment with AI images and video, the onus is on them to establish permissions from creators and properly attribute their use, to avoid individual copyright cases.

The news: California Governor Gavin Newsom signs AI safety law.

Why it matters: It’s the first in-nation law that forces developers at major US-based AI companies to publicly disclose their AI safety and security protocols, and includes whistleblower protections for AI workers, in what analysts are saying could set a benchmark for other states to follow. But it also moves in direct opposition to Trump’s recent AI action plan, which all but deregulates the development of AI at these companies on a national level. As the state that houses much of the Silicon Valley tech companies at the forefront of AI development, California is the closest to their inner workings, but brands operating at a national level will need to watch how other regional governments react, and if this policy influences the ongoing regulation battle at a federal level.

The news: OpenAI launches ChatGPT Checkout.

Why it matters: Instant Checkout removes the friction for ChatGPT users — where they previously searched and discovered products on ChatGPT, before clicking through to make the purchase on a brand’s own site, this new feature omits that final step, shortening the purchase journey. It has big implications for brands’ partnership decisions, advertising strategies, and how they design their websites to appeal to both human customers and LLM “crawlers”. Find out more about what it means for fashion here.

The news: Meta debuts three new AI smart glasses models, but demos fail.

Why it matters: At Meta’s annual Meta Connect conference on 17 September in California, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg unveiled the first AI smart glasses with an in-lens display, the Meta Display glasses, designed to replace the wearer’s need to get out their phone. But the live tech demos featured a couple of glitches. A demo of the AI glasses’ ability to interpret cooking ingredients in front of the lenses and give the wearer recipe instructions misinterpreted the selection of raw ingredients as a half-cooked dish, and the glasses failed to pick up a live Whatsapp video call demo between Zuckerberg and Meta CTO Andrew Bosworth.

Bosworth later took to Instagram to explain why the demos went wrong. It wasn’t down to the Wi-Fi, as Zuckerberg suggested onstage, but down to the amount of Meta AI glasses in close proximity during the demo, which caused a flood of traffic to Meta’s live AI server, according to Bosworth. It’s a reminder of just how many pieces of the puzzle are required for this nascent tech to function. At $799 a pop, consumers will expect their buzzy AI glasses to work, so Meta has its work cut out to fix any bugs before they become available for US consumers at the end of the month.

The news: US Federal Trade Commission launches inquiry into AI ‘companions’ used by teens.

Why it matters: Tech companies including OpenAI, Meta and Google are being probed by the US regulator over AI chatbots that provide “companionship”, after a series of high-profile suicides and harm among young people linked to their interactions with the tech. The US Federal Trade Commission (FTC) has ordered the companies to share information about how their AI chatbots develop characters and personas, and how they monetise this kind of engagement. It’s also asking tech firms to disclose what measures they have in place to avoid harm, especially among young people, and how they handle personal data from the conversations.

Given that a primary hesitation among luxury brands in their adoption of AI is the risk of losing consumer trust, the industry should watch the case closely. As user trust in conversations with generative AI grows, analysts say this trust will extend to other online activities like shopping. But as AI regulation becomes increasingly fragmented, more of the onus is on brands to develop their own guardrails. The results of the inquiry should provide key insights for brands that are grappling with developing their own AI ethics, and could inform industry standards in future.

The news: Fraudsters use AI to fake defects on resale platforms.

Why it matters: A disturbing trend has been called out on fashion social media this week — some buyers on resale platforms are using AI image generators to fake defects on received items to get refunds. On resale platforms, trust hangs in the balance between a seller’s description of their garment condition and what the item actually looks like. Although a number of the fake defect attempts called out on social media are amusingly bad, some are more realistic, thanks to recent improvements in AI image generators and their usage becoming more commonplace. When Vogue Business reached out to the main resale platforms, they said this was not yet a business concern — suggesting that this type of fraud is still in its infancy. But in order to retain trust, resale platforms will have to stay on the front foot of this new risk, which could mean investing in an enhanced verification process like videos for buyers making defect claims, which is an added cost for the platforms that could be passed onto users. Vinted told Vogue Business it is “closely monitoring the evolving use of AI among our members to ensure it remains consistent with the platform’s usage guidelines”.

The news: Shein appears to use an AI Luigi Mangione as a T-shirt model.

Why it matters: Shein has opened an internal investigation after the product image for a men’s shirt listing on its website featured a model that resembled Luigi Mangione, the person accused of killing UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson last year. The online retailer has now taken down the image, and told press in a statement: “The image in question was provided by a third-party vendor and was removed immediately upon discovery.” But the image was online long enough to be shared widely on social media, with speculation surrounding whether it was generated using AI. Mangione has amassed a cult following among some in the US who frame him as a folk hero, in opposition to the US healthcare system. This fuelled a surge of clothing emblazoned with Mangione’s face and name being sold online on retailers like Etsy and Ebay. Connecting the dots, this incident is a stark reminder of the importance of human oversight at brands experimenting with AI for more routine image needs like product listings. And it’s a very stark reminder of how undiscerning the AI image generators themselves are at this point — they crawl the good, the bad and the ugly of the internet to produce their images.

The news: Amazon launches Lens Live instant AI image scanning tool.

Why it matters: Amazon already had a visual search tool, Amazon Lens, which allowed customers to upload images or scan barcodes to discover products. But this new live component brings the retailer more in line with Google Lens and Pinterest Lens — shoppers can now point their phones at things they see before them in the real world, and Amazon’s app will suggest similar or matching products on its platform. The new feature will initially be rolled out to “tens of millions” shoppers in the US, and the company has not said when it will be rolled out to further US customers or into other markets. The live lens feature will also integrate with Amazon’s AI shopping assistant Rufus for more product information. It’s clear that Amazon is investing big in its AI-powered shopping features, and this represents the biggest multimodal search development on a retailer’s own platform thus far. How long until competitors follow suit?

Why it matters: The initial buzz around the launch of ChatGPT-5 and its “PhD-level” knowledge this month has wound down, amid criticisms of the update as somewhat underwhelming. Social media users, tech influencers and journalists abound have commented on the tool’s tendency to “hallucinate” as well as only marginal improvements in its natural language style. One thing that could benefit fashion, however, is OpenAI’s big new emphasis on health — the company wants users to consult ChatGPT like their doctor. But why does this affect fashion brands? Experts tell me that when users are confiding in the tool about their health, and it’s giving them useful recommendations, their trust in the tool will increase exponentially. Trust will likely then extend to other avenues, such as shopping queries and style advice. Let’s see how this plays out in the coming months.

The news: J Crew sparks backlash for unlabelled AI campaign imagery.

Why it matters: This week, newsletter Blackbird Spyplane published a visual investigation of J Crew’s latest campaign — the launch of a collab with Vans — in which the images gave a strong indication they’d been generated by AI. Spyplane managed to uncover the creator of the images — AI photographer Sam Finn. This sparked widespread backlash on social media and within fashion communities, partly because the brand hadn’t credited the use of AI for its images, and partly because, as Spyplane put it, J Crew had “used AI to counterfeit their own vibes”. The images in question resemble J Crew’s catalogue imagery from its late ’80s to early ’90s heyday, which made the use of AI for such an authentic vintage aesthetic even more puzzling to internet critics. The brand has yet to confirm its use of AI, but it did update the campaign instagram post to credit Finn for the “digital art”. (J Crew has not responded to Vogue Business’s request for comment on the campaign.) It’s the latest in a string of AI image controversies across fashion that shows just how thorny the issue is within creative communities. Is there a way that fashion brands can get AI images right?

The news: Meta partners with Midjourney on AI images and video.

Why it matters: Meta made its first move into AI image generation last year, when it launched image generation tool Imagine on its Facebook, Instagram and Messenger platforms. Now, it’s partnering with Midjourney — which is widely viewed as one of the best AI image generation tools on the market — to “bring beauty to billions”, according to chief AI officer Alexandr Wang. It’s the latest move from Meta in its huge AI investment push, and could now enable it to develop image and video products that compete with Google’s Veo and OpenAI’s Sora — and could impact the visual content consumers grow more accustomed to seeing on its social platforms.

The news: Meta is implementing an AI hiring freeze, according to a report from The Wall Street Journal.

Why it matters: After spending the past few months hiring over 50 AI researchers, Meta has hit pause, the tech giant confirmed to The Wall Street Journal. The hiring freeze coincides with a wider restructuring of Meta’s AI teams, which involves splitting them into four divisions. As AI becomes an increasing priority, businesses are not only competing in an AI talent war, but they are having to figure out the internal infrastructures, too. Already, investors are concerned about the stock-based compensation tech giants are offering AI talent, which could dilute shareholder value.

The news: Google adds agentic capabilities to AI Mode search function.

Why it matters: The agentic update allows AI Mode to make restaurant reservations with multiple constraints and preferences (“I only have an hour and need a quick lunch spot, any suggestions?”). The feature will soon expand to local service appointments and event tickets. The update signals a major step towards AI assistants functioning as agents and navigating real-world systems, rather than just a smart search engine. AI Mode has previously only been available in the US, the UK and India, but now Google has rolled it out to over 180 additional countries.

The news: Meta is offering AI translations for creators to expand their global reach.

Why it matters: Meta AI translations — a tool that dubs and lip-syncs reels on Facebook and Instagram into another language — will now be available for English to Spanish and Spanish to English translations, with further languages in the pipeline. The move has the potential to help creators grow audiences in new markets, boosting the creator economy even further.

The news: ChatGPT-5 launches for businesses.

Why it matters: Hot on the heels of OpenAI’s rollout of ChatGPT-5 to consumers and developers last week, the company has extended the model to its enterprise customers. Spanish bank BBVA and Zara owner Inditex have already adopted the updated tool — Inditex data and AI lead Oscar Mateos took to LinkedIn to say, “GPT-5 feels less like a tool and more like an expert collaborator who’s always one step ahead.” Who will be the first luxury conglomerate to adopt the upgraded tech?

The news: Stitch Fix announces AI shopping updates in personalisation push.

Why it matters: Stitch Fix is seeking a competitive edge as several dedicated, AI-powered personal styling startups burst onto the scene — including Daydream, which was founded by former Stitch Fix COO Julie Bornstein, and has so far raised $50 million in funding to support its development. Stitch Fix has previously deployed AI to understand personal style and predict trends, but claims that a new suite of AI-powered personal styling features will “increase personalisation, convenience and inspiration” for its users. The updated features include: an AI style assistant for customers, which uses generative AI to suggest outfit inspiration based on the taste profile it builds from their data over time; a “Stylist Connect” platform for customers to chat to human stylists; virtual try-on “personalised AI style visualisation”; and AI design integration for its private brands.

The news: OpenAI launches ChatGPT-5, touting its knowledge as a “major upgrade” from ChatGPT-4.

Why it matters: We’ve been waiting for this update for a while (the last GPT-4 update was in March 2023), and the developments within OpenAI’s technology are a key indicator of how far AI has come, and what brands should know it can do. In OpenAI CEO Sam Altman’s words, “GPT-3 sort of felt like talking to a high school student, GPT-4, maybe it was like talking to a college student. But with GPT-5, now it’s like talking to an expert, a PhD-level expert in anything, any area you need, on demand.” OpenAI also says its new model beats the LLMs from competitors Google, X and Anthropic. Perhaps most interestingly for brands, Open AI says the new model is more conversational than ever, which could have implications for customer interactions with their brands both in ChatGPT search for shopping, and their chatbot interactions.

The news: Pinterest CEO pitches the platform as an “AI-enabled shopping assistant”.

Why it matters: In the company’s second-quarter earnings call, Pinterest CEO Bill Ready said the app’s users don’t necessarily think of it as a shopping platform, but that its experiments with AI mean they’re actually getting proactive recommendations for products that “align with their taste and their style, the way a really great personal shopping assistant would”. Ready said the platform is also using multimodal AI (combining text and images), AI for visual search, and AI for conversational search. It’s one to watch for brands, as consumers move to more niche social platforms for product discovery.

The news: Google says AI search is increasing, not decreasing, traffic to websites — but doesn’t share data to back up its claims.

Why it matters: Some industry analysts suggest that the rise in AI-powered conversational search is decreasing organic traffic to websites. This week, Google rebuffed these claims as “inaccurate”. “Average click quality has increased and we’re actually sending slightly more quality clicks to websites than a year ago (by quality clicks, we mean those where users don’t quickly click back — typically a signal that a user is interested in the website),” Google’s head of search Liz Reid wrote in a blog post. Yet the blog cited no data — and the reports it was challenging do. Google isn’t the only AI-powered search engine, either. ChatGPT is increasingly being used for consumers’ shopping searches. AI optimisation is emerging among marketers to try to increase their sites’ chances of appearing in search — here’s what brands need to know about the nascent practice.

The news: Mark Zuckerberg says those without AI smart glasses will be at a “significant cognitive disadvantage” in future.

Why it matters: Meta had a big week last week, beating revenue and profit expectations in its second-quarter earnings. It’s good news for CEO Mark Zuckerberg, who has been investing heavily in AI, and will be wanting to reassure investors that the company is in a position to do so. Zuckerberg seized the good news opportunity to go in even harder on the company’s AI ambitions. Not only did he announce that the company’s AI models will soon reach human-like “superintelligence”, but he reinforced his belief that AI-powered glasses will be the primary way humans interact with AI in coming years.

“I continue to think that glasses are basically going to be the ideal form factor for AI," Zuckerberg told investors on the earnings call. “I think in the future, if you don’t have glasses that have AI — or some way to interact with AI — you’re probably going to be at a pretty significant cognitive disadvantage.” Meta has something of a first-mover advantage in the world of smart glasses, but Google, OpenAI and Apple are among the other Big Tech players investing in wearables’ AI promise. Read more about Meta’s smart glasses moves here.

The news: Experts say AI is developing much faster than expected.

Why it matters: We’re used to tech CEOs shouting about the potential of AI. But when experts including Nobel Prize winner Geoffrey Hinton say the technology is developing much faster than they ever anticipated, it adds even more fuel to the fire. Examples of AI models’ accelerating developments are everywhere: this week, Meta’s model began correcting itself.

Since Trump more or less deregulated the sector in the US, there’s barely anything standing in these companies’ way. This means global brands need to get to work on developing internal AI guardrails, especially if they’re handling lots of consumer data across jurisdictions (like the EU) that are stricter on AI.

The news: Apple says it is “very open” to acquisitions this year to catch up to competitors on AI.

The news: Google launches AI shopping mode in the UK.

Why it matters: Google launched its AI Mode search feature for shopping in the US in May, and the UK rollout this week indicates its plans to expand the number of consumers who shop using the feature — and fast. AI Mode uses Google’s generative AI tool to produce a chat-style interface for users, giving them a conversational search experience in which they can converse back and forth, and ask more specific questions. Three other AI shopping features rolled out on Google in the US — virtual try-on, Gemini-powered personalised shopping recommendations, and agentic price-match comparisons — are yet to be announced in the UK.

It’s particularly relevant for shopping. Some 80 per cent of consumers now rely on AI-written results for at least 40 per cent of their searches, according to Bain & Co. All this means ad agencies and marketing teams have shifted their focuses from SEO (search engine optimisation) to what’s been coined “AIO” (AI optimisation). Learn more about emerging AIO practices in fashion here.

The news: UK government signs “strategic partnership” with OpenAI in AI investment push.

Why it matters: The UK is eager not to get left behind in the so-called ‘AI race’ between the US, Europe and China, and this is the latest sign it’s keen to attract more investment to Britain’s AI sector. The government’s plans to use more of OpenAI’s technology to deliver public services will likely mean that the technology is trained on citizen data. In turn, OpenAI is planning on hiring more UK staff for its research and engineering teams, and increasing the size of its London office, as per the plan. ChatGPT maker OpenAI is currently one of the most powerful companies in the world, and President Trump’s new AI Action Plan shows how eager each government is to persuade the tech company — and its competitors — to develop their tech on their soil.

The news: Trump unveils US AI Action Plan and signs three AI executive orders.

Why it matters: The 28-page ‘AI Action Plan’ aims to build out the country’s AI infrastructure, cement America’s dominance in the industry and prohibit all federal agencies from using AI contractors that don’t comply with the White House’s definition of “ideological neutrality”. The new policies reverse several Biden-era federal AI safeguards related to DEI (diversity, equity and inclusion) and climate change, block state-level regulations on AI and further relax export rules so that global companies rely deeper on US-built AI. The move to get rid of existing AI regulations places further onus on individual companies to establish their own AI guardrails, especially if they operate across countries and jurisdictions. The US-centric policy also presents key challenges for fashion’s global supply chain and consumer base, which you can read more about here.

The news: OpenAI has shown some brands a pilot of a checkout feature that would enable users to complete purchases within its ChatGPT platform, according to a report by the Financial Times. It would charge brands commission for sales made this way.

Why it matters: When users search for products, ChatGPT currently shows recommendations with links to click through to brands’ own e-commerce sites. Bypassing this step opens up a clear revenue stream for OpenAI, but could significantly impact brands’ online sales. Those whose websites are picked up easier by ChatGPT would hold a significant advantage over those whose aren’t. No one’s quite sure what makes large language models (LLMs) like ChatGPT tick yet, but there are some key practices emerging that could help brands optimise for AI search.

The news: WeTransfer has U-turned on plans to use UGC to train AI, after a revision in its terms of service caused widespread backlash.

Why it matters: Copyright protection has long been in place to safeguard creatives like photographers against their work being used without permission. Tech companies’ training of AI models on their work is proving a thorny issue within the fashion and creative industries, as it poses a risk of copies, duplication and direct competition — ultimately threatening their source of income. Given that WeTransfer is widely used within the creative industries, the company’s U-turn represents the perceived reputational risk that openly training AI models on creative work can cause.

The news: Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg has said the company will build a data centre “the size of Manhattan” to fuel its planned development of AI products.

Why it matters: It’s the latest in a string of moves from Meta — which owns Instagram, Whatsapp and Facebook — that demonstrate the scale of the investment it’s making in developing AI products. Data centres are hugely expensive to build and maintain, and the size of what Zuckerberg is suggesting would cost billions of dollars. Zuckerberg has been very bullish on the potential for the company’s AI smart glasses in particular, and talk of Meta buying a stake in its Ray-Ban Meta AI glasses co-creator EssilorLuxottica has intensified in the last month.

#6716. The True Story of Ian Charleson, the Trailblazing Actor Andrew Scott Plays in Elsinore

In Elsinore, quite possibly this year's most moving film, Andrew Scott gives a captivating, awards-worthy performance as the late, great Scottish actor Ian Charleson. Though he never became a household name, Charleson's star shone brightly in the early 1980s when he appeared in two consecutive Best Picture winners: 1981's Chariots of Fire and 1982's Gandhi.

"I'd rather die of Hamlet than die of AIDS," Scott-as-Charleson says in Elsinore, which opened in select theaters last week. This defiant line sums up the incredible coup de grâce that Charleson pulled off at the end of his life. When he began his valedictory stage run as Shakespeare's Danish Prince in October 1989, the 40-year-old actor was dying of AIDS. His face was so swollen with septicemia that the cast, crew, and audience at London's National Theatre were told he was recovering from a sinus operation.

"I begged him not to do Hamlet. I said to him, It will kill you, which it did," Charleson's friend Sean Mathias, an accomplished actor and director in his own right, told me. "The amount of energy it takes to play that kind of classical role, both physically and spiritually, would tire the most ardent athlete. For a man dealing with the onslaught of AIDS, it was almost impossible."

But against the odds, Charleson turned in a monumental performance. In a review for The Sunday Times, theater critic John Peter described his Hamlet as "virile and forceful" and wrote that the actor "oozes intelligence from every pore." Charleson's performance was all the more remarkable because he was an eleventh hour replacement for Daniel Day-Lewis, who left the production early—quite literally, midway through a performance—because he was so haunted by Shakespeare’s gothic tragedy.

"People still remember Ian's performance as Hamlet," says Andrew Scott, whose performance in the film captures Charleson in the tumultuous final year of his life. Elsinore's screenwriter Stephen Beresford believes it's fitting that no footage of Charleson's defining performance exists. "An important thing to remember about Ian is his extraordinary contradictions," he says. "He wants to be seen and not seen, to be known and not known." Charleson, in fact, was so publicity-averse—perhaps partly because he was a closeted gay man—that he walked out of the Chariots of Fire press junket.

At the same time, he was simply an old-school British thespian who believed that the work should speak for itself. "Ian was incredibly passionate about this extraordinary part of Hamlet," Scott adds, citing the actor's devotion to his craft as a major incentive in his decision to join Elsinore. "But the chief thing [I love about him] is his courage and sense of humor."

In Elsinore, we see Scott's Charleson share his AIDS prognosis with his Hamlet castmates. When he died on January 6th, 1990, just seven weeks after his final curtain call, it was also disclosed to the public at large. At the time, Charleson's close friend Ian McKellen told the British press: "It is rare for anyone in the public eye to say that they are HIV positive, let alone that they have AIDS. It is a tribute to Ian that he should ask for the cause of his death to be made public and it is the most marvelous offer of support that he could have given to other men and women all over the world suffering from the AIDS virus."

Beresford, who wrote Elsinore's screenplay after extensive conversations with Charleson's friends, family, and contemporaries, told me that it was actually the actor's father, Jack, who made the decision to disclose his cause of death publicly. "The tabloids were already circling, so I think there must have been fear that it was going to come out anyway," suggests Beresford, who previously penned the 2014 film Pride, which told the true story of gay and lesbian activists who raised money for the families of English coal miners during their 1984 strike.

Still, even if it wasn't carried out at his own behest, Charleson's posthumous contribution to HIV/AIDS awareness was very significant at a time when the disease was highly stigmatized and virtually impossible to treat. It would be another five years before HAART (highly active antiretroviral therapy) made the disease manageable.

In the U.K., the actor has also been immortalized with the annual Ian Charleson Awards, which since 1991 has recognized the best classical stage performances by actors under the age of 30. Past winners include David Oyelowo, Andrea Riseborough, Paapa Essiedu, Rebecca Hall, and Jack Lowden, while Benedict Cumberbatch, Cynthia Erivo, and Jessie Buckley have all received runner's-up prizes or commendations. "Ian's name is legendary within the [British] theater because of what he achieved in Hamlet, and the awards were set up to keep his memory alive," Beresford says.

In Elsinore, we see Scott's Charleson wryly lamenting the fact that, though he starred in the Oscar-winning Chariots of Fire, "all anyone can ever remember is its theme music." In this stirring sports biopic, Charleson played Eric Liddell, a devout Christian who managed to win gold at the 1924 Olympic Games despite withdrawing from his best event, the 100-meter sprint, because the heats fell on a Sunday. Charleson also appeared in the following year's Best Picture winner, Gandhi, as an Anglican priest who supported the iconic title character's fight for Indian independence.

Sadly, despite these back-to-back triumphs, Charleson never made it as a bona fide movie star. By 1986, he was reduced to appearing in Car Trouble, a crass British comedy about a man who falls in love with his new convertible. "He was very disappointed that film stardom didn't prolong itself," says Mathias, who believes that Charleson's sexuality denied him further opportunities in mainstream movies. "He wasn't out [publicly], but everyone in the business knew he was gay. And back then, gay actors just weren't given work in Hollywood."

Consequently, and perhaps aptly given his predilection for the stage, Charleson found salvation in the theater. On June 25th, 1989, he appeared in a one-night only revival of Martin Sherman's seminal queer play Bent. This pointed production at London's Adelphi Theatre, which also starred McKellen, Ralph Fiennes and Richard E. Grant, was staged to raise money for The Stonewall Group, a newly formed nonprofit that went on to become the U.K.'s leading LGBTQ+ rights organization. Charleson portrayed Greta, a drag performer who changes into male-presenting clothes during the play.

By this point, Charleson's torso was covered in lesions caused by Kaposi's sarcoma, a rare form of cancer common in AIDS patients. Mathias, who was directing the fundraiser, had screens erected on stage so that Charleson could change costumes out of view. "Ian said to me, But the crew can still see my body from the wings! So I said I'd get more screens put up," Mathias remembers. "But then he thought about it, and went, You know what? Fuck it! I always feel that was the moment, really, that he decided he would come out [as having AIDS]."

Shortly after Bent, Charleson was asked by Hamlet's director, Richard Eyre, to step in for Daniel Day-Lewis. Dickie Beau, an actor and writer who paid tribute to Charleson with his one-man stage show Re-Member Me (and who appears in Elsinore as the drag activist Sister Belladonna), believes Bent is a "truly significant" part of his legacy. “Not only did it help to kickstart [the charity] Stonewall, but it said a lot about him that he was happy to play Greta, who isn't a leading part,” he says. "Ian McKellen once said to me that, as much as Charleson saw himself as a lead actor, he was also a company man."

It's another of the fascinating contradictions that seem to make up Ian Charleson. Mathias says he was generally "quiet and private" and "very masculine," but also possessed a "wonderfully camp sense of humor." There's a poignant irony in his becoming the subject of a major motion picture, Beresford says, laughing: "Ian would have hated this publicity tour. I can guarantee that absolutely no part of him is watching us today!"

For Scott, who embodies Charleson so beautifully that he’s considered an awards season frontrunner, Elsinore's purpose is simple: “I hope our movie continues his legacy.”

#6715. Maple Bourbon Chicken With Brussels Sprouts

If you, like most people, hear the term “bourbon chicken” and have no idea what it is, let me call it by its more common name: toothpick chicken. Yes, the suspiciously delicious chicken shelled out at mall food courts on toothpicks is most likely bourbon chicken. Popular at American Chinese or Cajun-style Chinese restaurants, the sticky-sweet chicken is the utter definition of delicious, luring weary shoppers into food courts to find refuge from the bubblegum pink sweatpants and ripped denim. This version takes cues from the classic but swaps in some autumnal ingredients to make it fit for the season. Charred brussels sprouts leaves and pecans add bulk, while maple syrup and apple cider vinegar give it that delightful tart-sweet flavor we know and love. Serve it over rice or noodles or all by its lonesome for a hearty dinner that will take you back to the '90s.

More chicken dinner winners here: Sheet-Pan Hot Honey Chicken and Peaches; Basil Chicken Stir-Fry; and Ginger-Garlic Chicken and Vegetable Stir-Fry.

Whisk one 1½" piece ginger, peeled, finely grated, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, ⅓ cup bourbon, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, ¼ cup apple cider vinegar, ¼ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes, 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, ¼ cup low-sodium soy sauce, and ½ cup water in a small bowl to combine. Set sauce aside.

Toss 1½ lb. skinless, boneless chicken breasts, halved crosswise, thinly sliced against the grain, remaining 1 Tbsp. cornstarch, and remaining 1 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce in a medium bowl until chicken is coated; set aside.

Heat 2 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a large skillet over medium-high. Add 1 lb. brussels sprouts, halved through stems, leaves separated, and cook, stirring very occasionally, until just tender and blackened in spots, about 5 minutes. Transfer to another medium bowl.

Add more oil if pan looks dry and, working in batches if needed, arrange reserved chicken in a single layer and cook, turning occasionally, until golden brown and cooked through, about 5 minutes. Transfer to bowl with brussels sprouts.

Add reserved sauce to same pan and bring to a simmer. Cook, stirring constantly, until thickened, about 1 minute. Remove pan from heat and return brussels sprouts and chicken to pan; top with 1 cup salted roasted pecans, coarsely chopped. Toss to coat in sauce. Serve chicken and brussels sprouts with steamed white rice if desired.

#6714. How the Holy Is Revered and Corrupted in The Body

Netflix’s buzzy new show, created by Quinn Shephard, examines guilt, God, and control through the eyes of teen girls attending a Catholic high school

I wanted nothing more than to see the Holy Spirit. One day after church, my grandfather described the moment he first believed was witnessing the Holy Spirit: a soothing, cleansing sensation in which God, in some way, possessed and reassured your mind. Divine intervention felt attainable for a moment. At first, I, too, hoped to discover serenity, an especially enticing thought since my parents were far less religious. But over time, that belief twisted in my preteen mind, instilling instead a fear that every misstep might damn me. To be viewed unfavorably by God—as a kid—is a terrifying thought. And it lingers.

I soon let go of the institutionalized beliefs. Yet, a longing to believe in something greater—especially when facing the unknown—never fully left me. I still desired to find spiritual ground, one free from this all-consuming, stress-fueling shame. This friction between spiritual surrender and self-actualization is the beating heart of Quinn Shephard’s The Body. Beneath a relentless downpour of religious guilt and an insatiable appetite for forgiveness, the students at St. Mark’s Catholic High School battle their inner demons as they discern what they want for themselves versus what the world expects of them.

Shephard and co-showrunner Gina Gammell thrust the audience into an age of Razor flip phones, AOL instant messaging, and Juicy Couture tracksuits, all set to a 2000s soundtrack featuring Kylie Minogue and No Doubt. Its barbed-edged storytelling draws comparisons to Cruel Intentions and Pretty Little Liars, with a bewitching touch of Jennifer’s Body or The Crucible. Here, girl teenagedom traverses suppressed sapphic love and the systemic weaponization of religious guilt—an incisive critique biting enough to solicit a petition with over 120,000 people pushing to cancel it. This coming-of-age series emerges from the dual nature of what we hold sacred: its capacity for reverence and its vulnerability to corruption.

Catholic school scares me. Teenagers scare me more, especially Lisbeth (Geena Meszaros), the hyper-religious, manipulative student at the heart of the story. At first, The Body introduces us to Lisbeth as the quintessential “weird kid,” socially ostracized because of her eyebrow-less face and her freakishly religious family. (She evokes Carrie in Carrie.) But as The Body unfolds, Lisbeth pulls—or rather, tugs—at the web of guilt ensnaring the school’s dance team, the Lions, concerning the near-death of their new teammate, Grace (Sofia Wylie). Grace fell into a coma shortly after the girls pretended to sacrifice her at a Halloween party, popping ecstasy pills they referred to as the “body of Satan.” This hazing ritual is all in good fun until Grace’s heart actually stops … if only briefly.

The aftermath casts a shadow of guilt over everything—especially for Anya (Kristina Bogic), queen bee and dance team captain, who moved Grace’s unconscious body back to her bedroom with Lisbeth’s help. Soon after, Anya begins to see visions of Grace in her dreams. The moment she confesses this to the group, the other girls start confirming visions of their comatose friend. This uncanny groupthink preys on the girls with something to hide, who carry shame with them wherever they go. Anya, for instance, feels deep contrition for her romantic feelings for her best friend Elise (Sarah Boustany), whereas Elise more boldly embraces her queer sexuality. Elise faces the world with a steady confidence, shielding her from spiritual panic—and its subsequent manipulation.

The same isn’t true for most of her teammates, all of whom seek solace in the intangible, in God and the Holy Spirit, in the saintly visions of Grace. Grace then becomes a symbol of the sacred, a story that inspires people and therefore can be corrupted to control others. The girls’ desperate need for forgiveness makes them vulnerable to Lisbeth’s manipulation. When the team goes on a getaway together, they take hallucinogenic mushrooms before deciding that they must purge evil spirits from Grace by way of an exorcism (led by Lisbeth, of course). Lisbeth controls this ritual, forcing each girl to confess their sins. (She already knows them all after reading all their private messages.) Her feigned omniscience incites hysteria among the girls.

Shame clouds nearly all the girls’ minds. Maddie (Shirley Chen) wrestles with an eating disorder, some girls admit to premarital sex or impure thoughts, and Lisbeth attempts to squeeze out a confession from Elise about her feelings for Anya. The Body runs the gamut of teenage girlhood, but Shephard distills these insecurities into a single critique of control: how the holy—the fear of God—can exploit people, corrupt what we see, and shape what we believe. In episode 6, “Star Quality,” mass hysteria breaks out in the town, with people associated with the church now believing to see visions and revere Grace as a saintly figure. It’s driven by an innate desire to be seen—to see something—and a desperate desire to be part of something larger.

This same desire, to witness something collectively transcendent, forged the foundation of my spiritual beliefs. It also scared me enough to run from them. A connection to God came with fear of hellfire and the shame of sin. In this way, forgiveness felt like something I received out of desperation, rather than salvation. The Body studies the dangers of this unmitigated belief, of a doctrine designed to parse out the unknown. But by whose authority? Shephard’s story reminds us that the storyteller—the pastor or the manipulative teenage girl—controls the things we see and the things we may believe.

#6713. 25+ Best Bucket Bags Perfect for Everyday Wear

Some handbag trends come and go, but the bucket bag has proven its staying power. Somewhere between a slouchy hobo and a structured tote, the cylindrical style has long struck a balance between practical and effortlessly cool.

Part of the silhouette’s enduring popularity is its versatility. What began as a utilitarian design (one of the earliest iterations was a Louis Vuitton bag from the 1930s, originally intended to transport Champagne bottles) has become grounds for experimentation, with designers playing with proportions, materials, and distinctive details. This season, in particular, the bucket bag is enjoying renewed attention, with everything from cinched drawstring closures and sculptural top handles to unexpected hardware giving the classic a fresh look.

When shopping for a bucket bag, consider more than just the looks. Think about how and where you’ll carry yours: A spacious style can double as a work tote, while a mini version can add a touch of whimsy to evening looks. Fortunately, there’s no shortage of choices, whether you’re looking to invest in a luxury piece or discover something at a more accessible price point.

While preferences are unique to each shopper, the best options combine quality craftsmanship with functional details, from comfortable straps to secure closures and interiors that accommodate everyday essentials. Ahead, we’ve rounded up bucket bags to shop now, from understated versions to modern interpretations of the timeless silhouette.

Few materials make a handbag feel as luxurious as suede, particularly in wintertime. In rich shades of chocolate brown, navy, and burgundy, the tactile surface exudes sophistication. Just remember that suede requires care, particularly when water is involved.

For anyone who carries their entire life in their handbag, oversized bucket bags offer a stylish alternative to traditional work totes, with enough room for a laptop, water bottle, and whatever else the day demands. Supple leather designs have a relaxed, lived-in appeal, while sturdier versions offer a professionally glossy finish. Look for a wide strap, a secure closure, and an organized interior to make the most of the extra space and keep it gentle on your shoulders during the commute.

There’s something undeniably charming about a drawstring closure, which gives bucket bags their signature gathered appearance (and helps keep belongings secure). The cinched opening creates visually impactful folds that look particularly elegant in buttery leather, soft suede, or evening-ready satin.

If your wardrobe leans minimalist, a structured bucket bag may be the perfect match. Unlike softer iterations that collapse when set down, these styles maintain their architectural structure thanks to firmer leather and well-constructed bases; longer straps also allow for crossbody wear. Their shape makes them feel more like design objects than everyday accessories, especially when finished with distinctive hardware.

Good things really do come in small packages, and mini bucket bags are proof. These scaled-down versions trade generous storage space for playful proportions that are ideal for evenings out, weekend plans, or occasions when you only need the essentials. Choose a style with a detachable strap for added versatility, or carry it by hand for a more dressed-up effect.

Woven bags have moved beyond their beach-vacation beginnings. Intricately interlaced leather lends the bucket silhouette an artisanal quality, while tightly bound raffia in darker shades is appropriate for city dressing. Look for details like leather handles and tonal finishes that give these textured designs a more elevated, winter-ready look.

For a ladylike approach to the bucket bag, consider a top-handle silhouette. Short, sculptural handles give the otherwise casual shape a more refined appearance. Some feature rigid circular handles, while others have softly curved leather straps that sit comfortably in the crook of the arm.

#6712. Let Your Thanksgiving Tablescape Inspire Your Outfit

From cranberry velvet to bird motifs, holiday dressing starts at the table.

Every item on this page was chosen by an ELLE editor. We may earn commission on some of the items you choose to buy.

It finally feels like we’re in the thick of fall. It’s just beginning to get cold enough to wear our favorite coats, all the leaves have turned graceful shades of red, yellow, and orange, and somehow, nothing feels as comforting as a hot cider cupped in the perfect pair of leather gloves. We’ve almost arrived at Thanksgiving, which officially marks the start of the holiday season.

When it comes to fashion, Thanksgiving is actually one of the best holidays for holiday dressing. There is ample inspiration to rework fall classics and experiment with new trends that have just recently been presented on the runways, like berry tones, antique Victorian-inspired style, or even statement coats. The weather (not too cold just yet, but cold enough to layer) also makes it a prime time to play with accessories, whether it be medallion belts or grandmacore-inspired tapestry bags.

So, this year, why not pull your Thanksgiving outfit inspiration directly from your tablescape? Aside from celebrating with friends and family, a decorative tablescape is one of the most fun parts of this holiday. Make a Pinterest board for both, and you’ll match: There’s nothing chicer.

Read on for some ideas for Thanksgiving tablescape-inspired outfits.

Look to Thanksgiving’s ultimate favorite hue and layer up juicy shades of it. Rich, stunning tones of saturated cranberry pop (and you’ll probably spot them on your plate, too). It gives you a dramatic look with low-key effort. Opt for mixed textures. Think: leather, velvet, silks, and satins all done in deep cranberry.

FRAME FRAME x Amelia Gray The Corduroy Gray Pants

It’s completely okay to be a little bit literal. In fact, it can actually make your outfit more fun. Consider traditional tablecloth textiles—gingham, plaid, and tartan—and make them a part of your look. You can use them as an accent (a scarf or the lining of a coat) or make them the main focus.

By now, we all know the Thanksgiving mascot as the turkey. And many editorial tablescapes incorporate some kind of turkey or autumnal bird. Bird motifs are both a trend and extremely seasonally accurate (and inspiring) for a Thanksgiving outfit, too. Go conceptual: bird prints, peacock feather patterns, winged jewelry, and feather trims are all visually interesting.

FARM RIO birds tree long sleeve maxi dress

Chan Luu Crinkle Techno Taffeta Feather Dress

The easiest Thanksgiving outfit (and tablescape) trick is to lean into the natural codes of Mother Nature. Accessorize your outfit and table with dark fall florals, leaf motifs, gourds and pumpkins, or atmospheric forest and woodland fall elements. There are so many different directions to go in. But when in doubt, think of berry tones and fun details like walnut-shaped clutches or mushroom motifs.

Lela Rose Floral Organza Embroidered Crepe Dress

Choose a swanning maxi dress in shades of rich pumpkin orange or saffron yellow; even better if it has a fall-ready-feeling textile trend like fringe or tassels (which can also be found on tablescapes). Match it to your décor and the fall foliage: Layer up rich shades of red, rust, terracotta, chestnut brown, olive green, caramel, and sienna.

#6710. What The Altruists Gets Right About Tech Scammers Like Sam Bankman-Fried

The math holding up Netflix’s The Altruists is simple. Anthony Boyle plays currently imprisoned one-time cryptocurrency king Sam Bankman-Fried, and Julia Garner plays Caroline Ellison, fellow momentary crypto royal and Bankman-Fried’s one-time romantic partner. Both actors cook so fearlessly that the show’s shortcomings recede into the background. What you’re left with is a tidy sum: two excellent performances that offer rich, vatic examinations of real-life figures. From these visions of Bankman-Fried and Ellison we get a glimpse into a crime and into a psychology.

Famously, no bankers were sent to prison in the aftermath of the 2008 financial crisis. No suit from Countrywide Financial walked the yard in Lompoc. But Samuel Bankman-Fried did go to prison after being found guilty of wire fraud and conspiracy. For the Bloomberg set, his trial was covered as intensely as O.J. Simpson’s, and each day of it hit trip wires: polycules, blockchain, non-fiat currency, etc.

One of the threads in the journalism about the crimes, and on The Altruists, is that our power couple did not feel good in fancy spaces. But unlike the protagonists of so many other shows and movies from the tech-disruptor-story boom of the past 15 years, neither Boyle’s SBF nor Garner’s Ellison lean into rage.

On The Altruists, SBF and his inner circle frequent a Margaritaville in the Bahamas. They seem happy there, or at least at home. To be wildly rich, extremely young, and crushing vegan nachos at Jimmy Buffett’s theme restaurant is a choice made out of avoidance.

The show’s first episodes make clear the overlaps between Ellison and Bankman-Fried. They were true math minds surrounded by the glib Wharton crowd, goofs with board games. They were not-conventionally-attractive people in an industry where many people are quite hot, and where the primarily hot at least know which regression tool best fits what task.

The Altruists’s versions of SBF and Ellison found love in a hopeless place. Boyle interviews Garner for a position at Jane Street and they realize they have the exact same investment strategy—all in, all the time. If you didn’t know better, you’d be rooting for these two off-putting lovebirds to make a go of it.

Boyle’s performance mesmerizes. He seems to have control over his lashes, so completely articulated is his eye acting. His whole posture changes as he takes up different roles in the story: a curious loser, a gifted rhetorician, an anxious boss, an ignored former lover. The show shifts from alienation in New York to crypto adventures in Hong Kong to the office-dorm hybrid of “The Orchid” in the Bahamas. Boyle owns the physical transformations, letting the glee of the Hong Kong era fester into the eyebags and stress-weight accrued (probably one of the more ethical uses of a bodysuit I can recall) in the scheme’s last days.

Garner, meanwhile, has entered rarified air as a TV actor. Over the course of her career she has given us a moody, adrift Gen X student (Kimmy on The Americans), a Millennial lady of rage trapped in her dumpy hometown (Ozark), and now two glimpses of the self-satisfied Zillenial scammer (Anna Delvey in Inventing Anna and The Altruists). Garner’s signature move as a performer is to fail to sublimate anger or distress. Her characters have their own idiosyncratic patterns of twitches and attempts at steely gazes. The brittle darkness inside each of them sings. Her TV career belongs next to those of Elisabeth Moss and America Ferrera and Walton Goggins. It is time that this was generally acknowledged.

The supporting cast is solid, with one particular highlight. In the middle of The Altruist’s eight-episode run, we get an entire episode focused on Sam Trabucco, a college bestie of SBF, a former Alameda Research co-CEO, and an early cooperator with federal prosecutors once the wheels started falling off.

Alex Lawther plays Trabucco and almost walks off with the show. Lawther’s slight frame and self-searching candor give each line of dialogue intimacy. I first saw Lawther on Andor, playing Nemik, idealistic proto-Rebel and truest of true believers, a character based on Lei Feng, the Chinese communist folk hero and soldier, who, like Nemik on Andor, died in a freak accident but left behind a diary of such pure faith that it became a recruitment tool for the revolution. (A recording of Lawther reading that manifesto from his diary—his voice reedy and prophetic—literally haunts Imperial high command at the end of Andor.)

In maybe my favorite scene of The Altruists, Trabucco and Ellison get dinner together. They talk and realize their childhood paths intersected and diverged across metro Boston—the same math competitions, the same tests. But their hometowns were quite different. She was from Newton. He was from Natick. If you’re from New England, that’s the only detail you need. (If you aren’t, I recommend Love Story and/or the novels of Dennis Lehane for background.) At that dinner, Lawther shares a deep, specific childhood memory of his father and Garner’s Caroline flinches without breaking eye contact, like she’s watching a recording of a natural disaster.

Sadly, the Netflix sins are here in full effect. The lighting is smeary and wildly off in many scenes. The music and sound mix could hardly be blunter. Even Oscar-nominated showrunner Graham Moore and talented directors like James Ponsoldt can’t lift dialogue that not-infrequently feels tailored to second-screen viewers: “They’re both off-the-charts math geniuses!”

The braided narrative can turn single episodes into distracting puzzle boxes. The form is designed to function the way a big juicy 10,000-word legacy-media reported feature does: You know the ending, so it takes a memorable reshuffling of moments and incidents to create something new.

But watching this gang of true believers and opportunists and criminally naïve teenage dream brains go from geographic zone to zone does carry emotional import. To them, and to The Altruists, the Bay Area has become a dated country club, a mirror image of The Social Network’s version of Harvard from the 2000s, back when the Bay Area promised something fresh. Post-Recession New York is greyscale normie central. Hong Kong and Macau blur together. The show ends in the Bahamas, a place that rich outsiders have always treated as both Eden and the afterlife.

I think the era of the tech-bro-scammer-titan show and movie is reaching its end. If its dawn was The Social Network, the unrepeatable, mesmerizing You Can See Everything might be the sunset. Gen X icons Aaron Sorkin and David Fincher once tried to get their heads around millennial narcissism and now millennial genius Nathan Fielder has transformed his time with a real-deal apex-predator narcissist into a Möbius strip of content.

The drama of The Altruists depends on the psychology of the people who believe in crypto as a kind of syncretic faith. The show avoids a technical delineation of crypto itself, which makes sense. (I’ve yet to encounter a crypto evangelist who can provide a transparent explanation of the asset class that is superior to this.) ExxonMobil sells you a product and it works. Glock sells you a product and it works. Crypto works in so much as its existence justifies its existence. There are no earnings reports. Value is vibes.

Whenever something is being marketed as the future, it’s usually just the past, accelerated. People made crypto into an alternative financial system because they were “outsiders” who wanted to “disrupt.” Now the crypto system wants to be held close to the bosom of the enduring US financial markets and bulge bracket banks. A bill that would have brought them closer, setting up a regulatory framework, nose-dived in the senate.

It sounds almost cowardly, like running home to mom and dad: We made a brave new thing better and cooler and freer than your corrupt old monetary system. A few years later: Let us back in and give us all the benefits of the old system! Get us in your PNC digital wallet, normie!

Bankman-Fried and Ellison are both the children of elite academics. To its credit, The Altruists pokes these Freudian pains. Bankman-Fried was raised by Stanford Law professors and chose MIT. Ellison was the child of MIT academics and chose Stanford. There’s self-belief in those exact choices. The children of faculty get a significant leg up in gaining admission at their parents’ institution. SBF and Ellison wanted to do something honest on their own, at least once.

My parents are retired professors. You learn early on that you cannot possibly replicate your parents’ careers. A child of a lawyer can have their parent’s career 2.0. Same if you have doctors for parents. But truly successful academics—and given the market today, you either are truly successful or you don’t exist—create niches built only for one.

Successful academics eschew any number of linear career paths and lucrative fields to burrow into zones of learning where they have to be singular, own every network and endure any marginal post (Oregon State, thou hast thy music, too). To make it to a top institution, you need luck and power and timing to dovetail your own research record and professional charisma. Many people make it to powerful banks and hospitals and law firms. But if you manage to get tenure at Berkeley, you might really be that special.

The track record of the children of academics I know is messy: deluded guys floating around Portland or Boston trying to jam their unreadable YA series into the world, an acquaintance who self-sabotaged a promising, morally-clear career as a social worker because they did not get a doctorate and let that arbitrary marker of value smother their self-worth for decades.

SBF and Ellison were expected to perform precocity at all times, but the minute that they stumbled, Dr. Mom or Professor Dad stepped in with the better therapists and better lawyers to set everything right. The last two episodes of The Altruists bubble over with dread. Paul Reiser and Robin Weigert play SBF’s parents, and Jennifer Grey plays Caroline Ellison’s mom. Each performance puts its own spin on enmeshment and infantilization. The parents are not the big bads here. But they are the judgmental elitists who analyzed when they should have listened, and who raised these world-class scammers.

There was a guy a little like me in high school. Like me, he was the child of academics and teachers. Like me, he was clever and capable, which might have been enough in another high school. But such minor skills were door prizes in our grand, old, dizzyingly competitive boarding school. We both loved De La Soul. We were both cut from the same teams. We were both contrarians who trafficked in equal measures of insight and anserine bullshit. I won’t pretend to have been good friends with the guy—it was the classic situation where young men who play similar roles in their respective circles repel each other like the same sides of different magnets. But I sympathized. It’s painful to know exactly why you are not near the top of an elite ecosystem and then having to go on living in it.

I imagined he might have a career adjacent to mine. I imagined that we might see each other in the late 2000s at a Babygrande Records release party or in the bathroom at Santos Party House. It did not play out that way. A few years ago, during the inevitable age-related transition from Facebook to LinkedIn, the guy’s face and name swum across my screen. He’s become a big deal in the crypto space. At one point, he rapped about crypto on crypto podcasts. On a class-wide group chat, as former classmates who had chosen to work in community health settings or on federally-funded research projects shared their pain after losing their jobs in the DOGE cuts, and as they voiced their concerns about what other digits of the American experiment would be severed next, this crypto dude commandeered the chat to brag about taking his company public. No child of an academic has ever missed a chance to make it about them.

One of the side effects of the world-gobbling narratives around A.I. (which gets its own Social Network moment in Luca Guadagnino’s imminent Artificial, with Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman) is that crypto already feels cringe—at best, a chrome decoration on the world-shaking machinery of LLMs and Deep Learning. The brave new world of private money that needed no society and no army behind it has become just another widget. The most vulgar people in the world trade meme coins with Turkish billionaire failsons. That Uber driver for whom you had great sympathy waits forever for a crypto ship that will never come into port. (Bankman-Fried, as it happens, was an early investor in Anthropic; it was reported last week that his shares, liquidated during FTX's bankruptcy, would be worth $35 to $37 billion in the wake of the AI lab's splashy IPO.)

If 2026 is the close of the tech-movie and tech-show era, then how do we square The Altruists? It has arrived at the end of something. It’s not perfect, maybe not even excellent, but it is effective and memorable, and provides a showcase for superb young actors. I wonder how many of these shows about tech founders, disruptors, optimists, hustlers and misanthropes will last. The paranoia of 70s American film evaporated in the desert of 80s escapism and the wry smirk of Ronnie Reagan. The thorny, violent prestige TV era begat the soft-clothes forever-childhood of Stranger Things and of Ted Lasso. Legacy cannot be legislated in advance. I hope viewers check out The Altruists, and appreciate its gumption in allowing love—the least efficient of emotions—to animate the story.

But maybe I’m wrong. Maybe I’ve been hustled by Boyle and Garner’s wonderful acting. Maybe my almost-instinct about the past 15 years of watching damaged young ladder-climbers and their digital dreams on screen is almost true: what will survive of us is coins.

#6709. Steak Bites With Spinach Couscous

A traditional steak dinner can feel like too much for a weeknight: too expensive, too likely to trip the smoke alarm, too fussy to cook to a perfect medium-rare. But cut a steak into bite-size pieces and suddenly it transforms into a quick-cooking protein that’s no more demanding than chicken breast or tofu. Rub the steak with the spices and make the quick no-recipe yogurt sauce a few hours ahead if it’s helpful with time management. To account for the extra liquid thrown off by the spinach as it cooks, the water-to-couscous ratio in this recipe differs from that often found on the back of the bag (or box) so measure accordingly.

More quick dinners this way: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps; Gochujang Chicken Stir-Fry; and Easy Fish Tacos With Spicy Sauce.

Place 1–1¼ lb. boneless New York strip steak (1–1½" thick), cut into 1" pieces, 1 Tbsp. dried oregano, 2 tsp. onion powder, 2 tsp. sugar, and 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a medium bowl; season generously with freshly ground pepper and toss to coat. Let sit at least 10 minutes or cover and chill up to 8 hours (no need to bring to room temperature before cooking if chilling).

Heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large high-sided skillet or medium Dutch oven with a tight-fitting lid over medium. Add 1 bunch scallions, thinly sliced, ½ cup finely chopped dill, 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; cook, stirring occasionally, until scallions are softened, about 5 minutes. Add 10 oz. baby spinach in 2–3 handfuls, stirring and letting wilt slightly after each addition before adding more, 5–7 minutes total. Pour in 1 cup water and bring to a boil; season with more salt if needed. Add 1 cup Moroccan couscous and stir to break up any lumps. Remove from heat; quickly cover with lid and let sit 10 minutes.

Meanwhile, heat 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a large skillet, preferably cast iron, over high. Arrange steak in a single layer; cook, undisturbed, until deeply browned underneath, 6–8 minutes. Reduce heat to medium; continue to cook, stirring often, until meat is just cooked through, about 1 minute more. Remove from heat. Add remaining 3 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and a large pinch of kosher salt; toss to combine. (Residual heat from pan will cook out any raw garlic flavor.)

Uncover couscous and fluff with a fork to separate grains. Spoon into a large shallow bowl or onto a platter. Top with steak. Cut 1 lemon into quarters and squeeze juice from 1 quarter over steak. Scatter thinly sliced cucumber and some dill sprigs on top; drizzle with oil.

Combine 1 cup plain whole-milk yogurt and a generous pinch of kosher salt in a small bowl; squeeze juice from 2 lemon quarters into yogurt. Stir to combine. If sauce is thick, stir in water, a spoonful at a time, to loosen.

Serve steak and couscous with yogurt sauce and remaining lemon quarter and more lemon wedges for squeezing over.

#6708. 52 Best Wedding After-Party Dresses for a Night to Remember 2026

All products featured on Vogue are independently selected by our editors. However, we may earn affiliate revenue on this article and commission when you buy something.

You’ve set the date and selected the ceremony gown; now, it’s time to consider your after-party look. This is your chance to loosen the rules and experiment with something less traditional. In fact, the best thing about a second (or third!) dress is the flexibility it offers: Keep things sleek and understated in a silky mini, or make a statement with sequins and embellishments. The hardest part may be settling on just one outfit for the dance floor. (A word to the wise: Be sure to choose the right shoes.)

Now for the fun part: We took a deep dive into all things bridal white—and metallic! and fringed! and feathered!—to bring you a range of styles for a standout after-party outfit change. You’ll find a mix of favorites from beloved bridal designers, including Danielle Frankel, Lein, Clio Peppiatt, and Vivienne Westwood. Browse minimalist picks from St. Agni and Róhe, vintage-inspired options from Dôen and Simone Rocha, and an iconic sequined mini by Rabanne—it’s practically built for the dance floor. Affordable pieces make the list, too: L’Agence’s ’90s-inspired maxi is a timeless choice, and Mango’s embellished slip is great for the bride who loves a bit of soft glam.

Below, shop our edit of the 52 best wedding after-party dresses—and get ready to celebrate in style.

Feathers, bows, and beading make for the most joyful kind of reception dress. Rachel Gilbert’s feather-hemmed mini is irresistibly flirty; Clio Peppiatt and Markarian scatter pearl beads and crystal appliqués across otherwise simple silhouettes. Consider it permission to be a little more daring once the vows are said.

Romance doesn’t have to end at the ceremony. Between Danielle Frankel’s silk mini, complete with a voluminous skirt, Givenchy's floral lace number, and Shushu/Tong’s bow-adorned dress, there’s plenty of reason to keep the aesthetic going after dark.

Bring the glitz to the after party in a metallic dress that’s guaranteed to keep all eyes on you. Simkhai, Ilkyaz Ozel, and Rabanne go all-out disco ball, covering their designs in head-to-toe sequins. Another route is Emilia Wickstead’s floral cloqué mini, which trades sparkle for a more subtle silver sheen.

It doesn’t take much to amp up a tailored silhouette. A row of three buttons adds a touch of whimsy to Self-Portrait’s soft yellow mini, while Aje opts for buttoned cuffs on its long-sleeve, bubble-skirt dress. Or, consider Destree’s fringed-thread mini if you’re after something unique.

For a second look with a nod to old-school romance, turn to silky fabrics, lace trim, and lingerie-inspired silhouettes. Dôen’s puff-sleeve midi is soft and feminine; Ganni’s luxe satin, boudoir-inspired style channels the glamour of time-honored nightwear; Posse’s floral-embroidered design brings a fresh, present-day spin to the look.

When the night stretches into the wee hours, something slinky, fitted, and, dare we say, risqué feels entirely appropriate. These pieces from Wiederhoeft, Fendi, Sir, and Alaïa pull out all the stops—you’ll just have to decide whether you want all-over sequins, something semi-sheer, or a sexy strapless option.

On the other hand, there’s no reason to wear something metallic and feathered if it’s just not in your style repertoire. Stay true to your minimalist aesthetic with clean-cut minis from Balenciaga and Solace London, or embrace slip styles with St. Agni and Róhe. All are pared-back, but just as party-ready as the rest of our list.

Few fabrics feel as undeniably bridal as glossy satin. L’Agence, Rixo, and Fforme offer understated polish for anyone on the hunt for a no-fuss dress. Elsewhere, Reformation channels Hollywood glam with a slinky halterneck maxi, tailor-made for a night of dancing.

Why save your “something blue” for your shoes or jewelry? These bridal dresses are an easy way to incorporate the adage. From Acne Studios’s slip silhouette to Galvan’s bias-cut satin mini and McQueen’s off-the-shoulder mini, consider keeping to tradition by way of a non-traditional after-party look.

Pull inspiration from the bridal bouquet; once the real one’s been tossed, you’re ready to celebrate hands-free. Khaite brings texture via rose-print jacquard fabric; Rat & Boa delivers an ethereal feel with its silk-tulle maxi that features an oversized, hand-stitched hibiscus; Magda Butrym adds a softer touch with a floral-inspired neckline.

Gathered detailing adds an artistic flair to otherwise simple shapes. Vivienne Westwood and Victoria Beckham carefully use draped corsets to accentuate the body. Stella McCartney and Liberowe take a different approach, relying on soft gathering to create a more effortless silhouette.

Ready to ditch the veil but don’t want to lose the drama for the after-party? Look no further than little white dresses with statement sleeves. Reiss’s mini fits the bill perfectly with its one-sleeved, draped design. For more excitement, go with Lapointe; there’s a bit of puffed-up volume in its feathered cuffs.

These dresses were made for the spotlight (and the photographer). Go long with Zara’s ’20s-inspired frock, turn heads with Staud’s pearlescent sequin mini dress, or keep it short, sweet, and trendy with Taller Marmo’s iteration. Each makes a strong case for choosing your second outfit based not just on how it looks standing still, but on how it moves once the music starts.
